la-marseillaise: On 25 April 1792 Baron Philippe Friedrich Dietrich, the mayor of Strasbourg and Worshipful Master of the local Masonic lodge, asked his guest Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle to compose a song that would rally soldiers from all over to defend their threatened homeland. That evening Rouget de Lisle wrote the Chant de guerre pour l'Armée du Rhin, War Song for the Army of the Rhine. Dietrich was executed the next year during the Reign of Terror. The lyrics reflect the invasion of France by foreign armies from Prussia and Austria that was under way, and Strasbourg itself was attacked a few days later. As most Alsatians did not speak French, a German version was published in Colmar in October 1792.

The melody soon became a rallying call of the Revolution. It was adopted as La Marseillaise after volunteers from Marseille, the fédérés, sang it in the streets by the end of May 1792. A young volunteer from Montpellier, François Mireur, had sung it at a patriotic gathering in Marseille, and the troops took it up as the marching song of the National Guard of Marseille. The fédérés entered Paris on 30 July 1792. The invading forces were repulsed after their defeat at the Battle of Valmy.

The Convention accepted it as the national anthem in a decree of 14 July 1795, France's first anthem. It lost this status under Napoleon I and was banned outright by Louis XVIII and Charles X, being reinstated only briefly after the July Revolution of 1830. Napoleon III's government brought it back during the Franco-Prussian War. In the 19th and early 20th centuries it was recognised as the anthem of the international revolutionary movement, and the Paris Commune adopted it in 1871 with new lyrics. It was reinstated as France's national anthem in 1879 and has remained so since.

Several antecedents have been suggested for the melody, among them a work by the Italian violinist Giovanni Battista Viotti, though it seems to have been published after the song, in 1795, and pieces by Mozart and by Jean Baptiste Lucien Grison. Hector Berlioz arranged it for soprano, chorus and orchestra about 1830, and Franz Liszt wrote a piano transcription. Robert Schumann quoted it in 1839 in a work for piano, although singing it was then forbidden in Austria as likely to cause public disorder, and Tchaikovsky quotes it in his 1812 Overture. Protesters used it in the Korean March First Movement in 1919, and Julián Felipe incorporated elements of it in the piece that became the Filipino national anthem.
la-pampa-province: La Pampa is a sparsely populated province in the Pampas in the centre of Argentina. It borders San Luis, Córdoba, Buenos Aires, Río Negro, Neuquén and Mendoza, and is larger than Austria, Taiwan, Ireland or Greece. Only two major rivers cross it, the Colorado, on the border with Río Negro, and the Salado, whose level has been dropping as its tributaries in Mendoza are diverted for irrigation.

The centre and east are a plain tilted gently towards the east, with a calcrete crust and cut by valleys running north-east to south-west. Some of these hold very large fossil inland dunes, and they now lie between the dry and humid Pampas. The province is mostly flat but has mountains such as the Sierra de Lihuel Calel, made largely of ignimbrite, a volcanic rock. The climate is temperate in the east and semi-arid in the west, and most rain falls in summer.

Hernando Arias de Saavedra was the first European explorer to reach the area, in 1604, and Jerónimo Luis de Cabrera explored it in 1662. Spanish colonists did not establish permanent settlements until the 18th century. Resistance by the local indigenous people prevented much expansion until the government of Juan Manuel de Rosas, and it ended only with Julio Roca's conquest of the desert in the 19th century. The territory was then divided among the officers, who built the first Argentine settlements.

The Territorio Nacional de La Pampa Central was created in 1884, with about 25,000 inhabitants and with territory that included the Río Negro Province and parts of other surrounding provinces. By 1915 it had 110,000 residents, a sign of the movement of settlers into the area. In 1952 the province's constitution was written and it was renamed after Eva Perón. In 1955, after the government changed and the Peróns went into exile, La Pampa and Chaco, which had been named for Juan Perón, took back their original names.

Cattle ranching is the most important agricultural activity and takes place across the province, while the more fertile north-east grows wheat, sunflower, maize and other cereals. The province also has oil and gas wells and deposits of sodium chloride, sodium sulfate and copper. Its capital is Santa Rosa, and it is divided into 22 departments. Visitors go to Lihué Calel National Park and the Parque Luro Provincial Reserve.
la-paz: La Paz lies in west-central Bolivia, 68 kilometres southeast of Lake Titicaca, in a canyon cut by the Choqueyapu River, in a bowl-like depression surrounded by the high mountains of the Altiplano. Overlooking the city is the triple-peaked Illimani, always snow-covered. At about 3,650 metres above sea level it is the highest administrative capital in the world, with a subtropical highland climate of rainy summers and dry winters.

The area had been the site of an Inca city on a major trading route. Spanish conquistadors entered it in 1535 but did not find La Paz until 1548. Pedro de la Gasca commanded Alonso de Mendoza to found a city to commemorate the end of the civil wars in Peru, and it was founded on 20 October 1548 as Nuestra Señora de La Paz, 'Our Lady of Peace', with Juan de Vargas as first mayor. The site first chosen was at the settlement of Laja, and a few days later the town was moved to the more clement valley of Chuquiago.

The city saw numerous revolts. In 1781 the indigenous leader Túpac Katari besieged it for six months before he was defeated. On 16 July 1809 Pedro Domingo Murillo began a revolution for independence, which marked the beginning of the Spanish American Wars of Independence. After the republican victory at Ayacucho in 1825 the city's full name was changed to La Paz de Ayacucho.

La Paz is the seat of government of Bolivia, with 755,732 residents in 2024, and a metropolitan area, including El Alto, of about 2.2 million. The presidential palace, the Palacio Quemado, and the legislature stand there, while Sucre, the constitutional capital, keeps the judicial power. The Plaza Murillo, the San Francisco Church, the Metropolitan Cathedral and Jaén Street preserve its colonial heritage. The Alasitas fair, held each year from 24 January, is on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
la-rioja: La Rioja covers part of the Ebro valley in the north and the Iberian Range in the south. The Ebro runs through the community for 120 km, and seven rivers flow towards it from the mountains, so that the region is sometimes called the Zone of the Seven Valleys. The name Rioja is generally taken to come from the river Oja, though other derivations have been proposed. It is first attested in 1099, in the Miranda de Ebro charter.

In Roman times the territory was inhabited by the Berones, Autrigones and Vascones. After the Muslim invasion of 711 it fell into Al Andalus. Most of it was reconquered in 923 by Sancho I of Pamplona, acting with the Kingdom of León and the Counts of Castile. La Rioja briefly formed the independent Kingdom of Viguera from 970 to about 1005, when it became part of the Kingdom of Pamplona. Sancho Garcés moved the capital of Pamplona to Nájera, and after the independence of Castile in 1035 the two kingdoms fought for La Rioja. In 1076, after the murder of Sancho IV, Navarre was divided between Castile and Aragon, Castile obtaining La Rioja.

The Navarrese under García Ramírez and his son Sancho VI fought Castile for its recovery from 1134, and the region was awarded to Castile in a judgement by Henry II of England and annexed in 1177. Its importance lay partly in the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela, which crossed the Ebro at Logroño. In 1833 a province of Logroño was formed.

In 1980 the province changed its name to La Rioja, and after the adoption of the Estatuto de San Millán in 1982 it was constituted as a single-province autonomous community. Its capital and largest city is Logroño. It is organised into 174 municipalities and borders the Basque Country, Navarre, Aragón and Castile and León. The region is well known for its wines under the Denominación de Origen Calificada Rioja.
la-rochelle: La Rochelle is a seaport on the Bay of Biscay and the capital of the Charente-Maritime department. Since the Middle Ages its harbour has opened onto a protected strait, the Pertuis d'Antioche, and the city has been regarded as a gateway to the ocean. Its western position saved days of sailing time and favoured fishing and trade across the Atlantic, even though it lies at no river mouth. The name was first recorded in 961 as Rupella, a Latin diminutive meaning little rock.

The Romans developed salt production along this coast, and villas and salt ponds of the period have been found. The harbour was established after Duke Guillaume X of Aquitaine defeated Isambert de Châtelaillon in 1130 and destroyed Châtelaillon's harbour. The city came under Plantagenet rule after Eleanor of Aquitaine married Henry Plantagenet in 1152, and it was the Knights Templar's largest base on the Atlantic. It traded with England, the Low Countries and Spain until Louis VIII captured it in 1224. It returned to the English in 1360 after the Treaty of Brétigny, and expelled them in June 1372.

La Rochelle adopted Calvinism during the Renaissance, and from 1568 declared itself an independent Reformed Republic on the model of Geneva. It sheltered Sea Beggars raiding Spanish shipping. After the St Bartholomew's Day massacre it endured a siege in 1572–1573, ended by the Peace of La Rochelle of 1573, which limited Protestant worship to Montauban, Nîmes and La Rochelle. Revolts against Louis XIII followed in 1622 and 1625. In the siege of 1627–1628 Cardinal Richelieu blockaded the city for 14 months despite an English expedition under the Duke of Buckingham; it surrendered and lost its mayor and its privileges. Louis XIV expelled 300 Huguenot families in November 1661.

The port prospered afterwards in trade with New France and the Antilles. Its shipowners took part in the triangular trade, dealing in enslaved people from Africa, sugar from the West Indies and Canadian furs. From La Rochelle the Carignan-Salières Regiment sailed for New France in 1665.

La Rochelle had 78,535 inhabitants in 2021 and is the most populous commune of its department. A bridge 2.9 kilometres long, completed on 19 May 1988, links it to the Île de Ré. It keeps a rich historical fabric, including the Saint-Nicholas tower, and has three ports for fishing, trade and yachting.
la-turbie: La Turbie is a commune in the Alpes-Maritimes department of south-eastern France, bordering the Principality of Monaco. It can be reached from Cap-d'Ail on the coast or by the Grand Corniche. A limestone outcrop above the village is called the Tête de Chien, or head of dog, a folk etymology from its former name Testa de camp, meaning head of a military camp. The commune once had wider boundaries and included the territory of Beausoleil, formerly Haut-Monte-Carlo, and of Cap-d'Ail, which was separated at the beginning of the 20th century. Only the old main town, around the remaining structure of the Roman trophy, forms the present commune.

In Roman times La Turbie lay on the Via Julia Augusta and was known for the Trophy of Augustus, also called the Trophée des Alpes, which Augustus made to celebrate his victory over the Ligurian tribes of the mountains, who had attacked merchants on the Roman trade routes. Much of the village is built partly of old stones taken from the ruins of the monument.

In the Middle Ages the village, then called Turbia, was mainly under the rule of the Republic of Genoa, and Dante wrote in the Divina Commedia that Turbia was the western limit of Italian Liguria. It belonged at times to Savoy and at times to the Principality of Monaco, from which its people took the Monegasque dialect, although the local Ligurian speech kept some features of the Niçois dialect of nearby Nice. That local dialect is nearly extinct, mainly since the inclusion of the Sardinian County of Nice in France in 1860.

La Turbie is regarded as the cradle of automobile mountain races. On 31 January 1897 the last stage of the Marseilles-Nice race was a 17-kilometre hillclimb between Nice and La Turbie, won by André Michelin in a steam-powered De Dion at an average of 31.8 kilometres an hour. The driver Wilhelm Bauer was killed there on 30 March 1900, the first driver killed in a hillclimb event, and the use of the course was banned after a second death in 1903, until the ban was lifted in 1909. From 1968 to 1995 nearly the same route formed the last stage of the cycle race Paris-Nice.

La Turbie is a commune of the Alpes-Maritimes that borders the Principality of Monaco. The Trophy of Augustus, also called the Trophée des Alpes, stands within the town and remains its best-known monument, and many of the village buildings are made from stones taken from its ruins. AS Monaco has had its training ground in an old quarry at La Turbie since 1981.
ladenburg: Ladenburg lies on the right bank of the Neckar, on the river's alluvial cone, about 10 kilometres from both Heidelberg and Mannheim. The Kandelbach flows into the Neckar south of the built-up area. The first settlement took place at some point between 3000 and 200 BCE, and the place began as a Celtic settlement called Lokudunom, meaning sea castle. In 200 BCE the Celtic centre of the region was moved there from the Heiligenberg near Heidelberg.

In 40 CE the Romans settled Suebian peasant militia, called the Suebi Nicrenses, and in 74 they founded an auxiliary fort with a camp village, the core of the later town. In 98 Emperor Trajan made Lopodunum a civitas and the capital of the Civitas Ulpia Sueborum Nicrensium. Around 220 it had a forum with a market basilica, temples, a theatre, baths and a town wall. With a walled area of about 32 hectares it was the largest Roman town in what is now Baden-Württemberg. Alamanni apparently destroyed it around 260. Valentinian I retook it in 369 and built a late antique harbour fortification, and Roman rule ended about the middle of the fifth century.

The Merovingians built a royal court there in 496, and in 628 the Frankish king Dagobert I gave the town and region to the diocese of Worms. In 1385 rule over Ladenburg was divided between Worms and the Palatinate after a bloody feud. In 1400 the citizens of Worms expelled their bishop, and Ladenburg became the bishop's seat. Under Bishop Johann III von Dalberg, from 1455 to 1503, it had its fullest flourishing. The Thirty Years' War brought partial destruction in 1622, and in 1705 Ladenburg fell wholly to the Electoral Palatinate. After Napoleon Bonaparte rearranged the political map of Europe it passed to Baden, and in 1849 the Neckar bridge was fiercely contested during the Baden Revolution.

The old town keeps half-timbered houses from the late Middle Ages, and St. Gallus Church has a south tower built in 1412 by Bishop Johann II von Fleckenstein. Carl Benz, inventor of the automobile, lived in Ladenburg from 1906 until his death in 1929, as did his wife Bertha, and the Bertha Benz Memorial Route passes through the town. An automobile museum bearing his name occupies the former factory buildings of C. Benz Söhne. Ladenburg marked the 1900th anniversary of its Roman city rank in 1998.
lahore: Lahore lies in the northeastern part of Pakistan, in central-eastern Punjab, with the Ravi River flowing on its northern side. It has a hot semi-arid climate, bordering on humid subtropical, in which June temperatures routinely exceed 45 °C and the monsoon rains arrive in late June. Its historic core is the Walled City in the northern part of the modern city, which was built piecemeal, with small cul-de-sacs, rather than to a geometric plan.

Early Muslim historians recorded the city's name in several forms, among them Luhawar, Lūhār and Rahwar, and no definitive record of its early history exists. The site has been inhabited for over two millennia, and Lahore rose to prominence in the late 10th century. Sultan Mahmud conquered it between 1020 and 1027 for the Ghaznavid Empire, and the governor Malik Ayaz rebuilt and repopulated the devastated city, erecting walls and a masonry fort in 1037–1040. It later served as a capital of several states, including the Delhi Sultanate.

Babur captured and sacked Lahore in 1525. Sher Shah Suri seized it in 1540, and Humayun reconquered it in February 1555. Mughal rule brought the most prosperous era of its history, and the city holds more Mughal-era monuments than Delhi or Agra. It was the capital under Akbar. In the 18th century Ahmad Shah Durrani occupied it in 1748 and invaded again in 1751, 1752 and 1757. The Bhangi Misl, a Sikh state, took it in 1767, and it later became the capital of the Sikh Kingdom of Lahore. Hazuri Bagh was built in 1818 under Ranjit Singh.

The East India Company seized control in February 1846 from the declining Sikh state, and the Punjab was annexed in 1849. At partition in 1947 the city's future was fiercely contested before the Boundary Commission; the 1941 census gave it a population of 671,659, 64.5 per cent Muslim. Partition weakened its economy, and Karachi rather than Lahore became the capital of Pakistan.

Lahore is the capital of the Pakistani province of Punjab and the country's second-largest city. It is a UNESCO City of Literature and a centre of Pakistan's publishing and of qawwali music. The Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981. Other landmarks include the Badshahi and Wazir Khan mosques and the Tomb of Jahangir. Punjabi is the most widely spoken first language.
lake-baikal: Lake Baikal lies in southern Siberia between Irkutsk Oblast to the north-west and the Republic of Buryatia to the south-east. It sits in a rift valley formed by the Baikal Rift Zone, where the Earth's crust is slowly pulling apart. The lake is 636 km long and 79 km wide, and its maximum depth is 1,642 metres. The rift is young and active, widening about 4 mm a year, and the area is seismically active. The lake has three basins, North, Central and South, drains into the Angara, and is among the clearest in the world. Its surface freezes from early January to early May or June.

The Baikal area has a long history of human habitation. At Mal'ta, some 160 km north-west of the lake, the remains of a young male known as Mal'ta Boy point to the Mal'ta–Buret' culture about 24,000 years ago. The Kurykans gave the lake a name that translates as much water; the Buryats later called it Baygal nuur, the natural lake. It lay in the former northern territory of the Xiongnu confederation and is one site of the Han–Xiongnu War, and Han records called it the North Sea, one of the semi-mythical Four Seas. It was under the Tang dynasty's Anbei Protectorate from 647 to 682.

Little was known to Europeans about the lake until Russia expanded into the area in the 1600s. The Baykalsk Pulp and Paper Mill, built in 1966 directly on the shore, discharged waste into the lake; Soviet scientists protested against it, and it closed in November 2008.

Lake Baikal is the deepest lake in the world, estimated at 25 to 30 million years old, and holds more than 1,000 plant species and 2,500 animal species, many of them found nowhere else, among them the Baikal seal, or nerpa. UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 1996. Buryat peoples live on its eastern side, where they raise goats, camels, cattle, sheep and horses.
lake-balaton: Lake Balaton is a freshwater rift lake in the Transdanubian region of Hungary. The Zala River provides the largest inflow of water, and the canalized Sió is the only outflow. The average depth is 3.2 metres. The lake affects the local climate, bringing about 5 to 7 centimetres more precipitation than most of Hungary and less extreme temperatures, and it freezes over in winter. The mountainous northern shore is a wine region, and the Mediterranean-like climate and volcanic soil have made the region notable for wine since the Roman period. The flat southern shore is known for its resort towns.

The Romans called the lake Pelso. The modern name is Indo-European in origin and derives from the Slavic word for mud or swamp. In January 846 the Slavic prince Pribina began to build a fortress and several churches near Zalavár, among forests and swamps along the Zala. His castle was the capital of the Lower Pannonian Principality, known as Blatnohrad or Moosburg, meaning Swamp Fortress, and served as a bulwark against both the Bulgarians and the Moravians.

The lake has long been important both tactically and culturally, and many folk tales surround it. During the Ottoman wars it helped defend Royal Hungary, and battles were fought there. Balatonfüred and Hévíz have long been resort centres for the Hungarian aristocracy. Only in the late 19th century did the middle class begin to visit, when landowners ruined by phylloxera in their vineyards began building summer homes to rent out.

Railways built in 1861 and 1909 increased tourism, and by the turn of the 20th century Hungarian biologists, geologists and hydrologists were researching the lake. The country's first biological research institute was built on its shore in 1927.

The last major German offensive of World War II, Operation Spring Awakening, took place in the region between 6 and 16 March 1945. Sepp Dietrich's Sixth Panzer Army and the Hungarian Third Army attacked, and the Red Army won. During the 1960s and 1970s government efforts made Balaton a major destination: overnight guests in July rose from 700,000 in 1965 to two million in 1975, many on subsidised trade union holidays. It also drew East Germans and other Eastern Bloc residents, and West Germans could visit, so that families separated by the Berlin Wall could meet there until 1989.

Balaton is the largest lake in Central Europe and one of the region's foremost tourist destinations. The major resorts are Siófok, Keszthely and Balatonfüred, and the Tihany Peninsula is a historical district. Keszthely has the Festetics Palace, and Badacsony is a volcanic mountain and wine-growing region.
lake-constance: Lake Constance consists of three bodies of water on the Rhine at the northern foot of the Alps: the Upper Lake, or Obersee, the Lower Lake, or Untersee, and the connecting stretch of the Rhine called the Seerhein. The Alpine Rhine enters from the south and the High Rhine leaves westward. The lake is 63 kilometres long, nearly 14 kilometres wide at most, covers about 536 square kilometres and lies 395 metres above sea level; its maximum depth, 252 metres, is in the middle of the Upper Lake. Its shoreline of 273 kilometres runs through Germany, Austria and Switzerland, and the exact location of the borders within the lake has never been settled between the three states.

The largest island is Reichenau in the Lower Lake. Lindau and Mainau lie in the Upper Lake, and the large peninsula of Bodanrück separates the two lakes. The largest towns on the Upper Lake are Constance, Friedrichshafen, Bregenz, Lindau, Überlingen and Kreuzlingen.

The lake was formed by the Rhine Glacier during the Quaternary glaciation. About 10,000 years ago, after the last glacial period, the Obersee and Untersee still formed one lake. Hunters and gatherers of the Mesolithic frequented the area without settling, and the first lasting settlements, pile dwellings and wetland villages, date from the middle and late Neolithic. A pile-dwelling village at Unteruhldingen has been reconstructed as an open-air museum. In 2015 a 20-kilometre line of about 170 man-made underwater stone mounds, dated to the Neolithic or early Bronze Age, was found near Bottighofen and Romanshorn.

The Roman geographer Pomponius Mela, around 43 CE, called the upper lake Lacus Venetus and the lower Lacus Acronius. Around 75 CE Pliny the Elder named both Lacus Raetiae Brigantinus after the main Roman town on the lake, Brigantium, later Bregenz, a name linked to the Celtic Brigantii. In English and the Romance languages the lake is named after the city of Constance, from the Roman emperor Constantius II, while the German name Bodensee derives from the village of Bodman.

The abbey island of Reichenau is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its three early medieval churches, and is also known for intensive cultivation of fruit and vegetables. The lake supplies municipal waterworks around its shores and the Bodensee-Wasserversorgung. The Alpine Rhine and the Seerhein do not mix greatly with the lake's water but flow through it on courses that change little.
lake-garda: Lake Garda lies between Brescia and Milan to the west and Verona and Venice to the east, cutting into the edge of the Italian Alps, and its shore is divided between the provinces of Brescia, Verona and Trentino. It is about 52 kilometres long and 16 kilometres wide, and its shape is typical of a moraine valley formed under a glacier.

The Sarca is its main tributary, and the Mincio, at Peschiera, its only outlet. In Roman times the lake was called Benacus, and some revered it as a god. The modern name derives from the town of Garda and from a Germanic word meaning place of guard, a trace of the Lombards. The mild climate supports olives, lemons and cypresses.

The strongest evidence of prehistoric settlement dates to the Bronze Age, when stilt houses stood in the lower lake. Romanisation took place mostly in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE. In 268 CE a Roman army under the future emperor Claudius Gothicus won a decisive battle over the Alamanni at the lake. The Roman presence is attested by villas, including the Grottoes of Catullus.

Under the Lombards the area was divided among the duchies of Brescia, Verona and Trento. In the 13th century the Scaliger family subdued the eastern shore, built the castles of Sirmione, Malcesine and Riva, and completed a fortified line called the Serraglio in 1355. Venice gained the eastern shore in 1405 and the western shore in 1426, and the 34 lake municipalities received ample autonomy.

In 1438 a fleet of six galleys and twenty-five ships was hauled over Monte Baldo by 2,000 oxen. After 1815 the lake belonged to Austria, in the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia. In 1943 the Italian Social Republic placed its ministries at Salò, Desenzano and other lake towns, and Mussolini's headquarters at Gargnano; Salò became its capital.

Around the lake lie 26 comuni, of which Desenzano del Garda is the most populated. The economy depends largely on tourism, which developed from the end of the 19th century, beginning with Gardone Riviera, where the poet Gabriele D'Annunzio built the Vittoriale degli Italiani, now a museum. Gardaland is the biggest Italian theme park, and Riva, Torbole and Campione are known for the winds that attract sailors and windsurfers. The rare carpione, a salmonid fish, is found only in the lake.
lake-huron: Lake Huron is shared on the north and east by the Canadian province of Ontario and on the south and west by the American state of Michigan. Hydrologically it is the eastern part of Lake Michigan–Huron, having the same surface elevation as Lake Michigan, to which it is joined by the wide and deep Straits of Mackinac. The main inlet is the St. Marys River from Lake Superior, and the main outlet is the St. Clair River, toward Lake Erie. It is split into five basins, including Georgian Bay, Saginaw Bay and the North Channel, and Manitoulin Island, the largest freshwater island on Earth, separates the North Channel and Georgian Bay from the main basin.

Its surface lies 176 metres above sea level, and it is about 332 kilometres long. With its 30,000 islands it has the longest shoreline of any Great Lake. Like the others, it was formed by melting ice as the glaciers retreated at the end of the last ice age, over a low depression once crossed by the now-buried Laurentian and Huronian Rivers.

About 9,000 years ago, when the water was approximately 100 metres below today's level, the Alpena-Amberley Ridge was exposed as a land bridge used as a migration route by large herds of caribou. Since 2008 archaeologists have found at least 60 stone constructions along the submerged ridge, thought to have been hunting blinds of Paleo-Indians. A 2013 underwater discovery confirmed that a trade network brought obsidian from Oregon almost ten thousand years ago.

On the eve of European contact, a town on or near the lake held more than one hundred large structures and between 4,000 and 6,000 people. The French, the first European visitors, often called the lake La Mer Douce, the fresh-water sea. A map of 1656 by Nicolas Sanson names it Karegnondi, a Wyandot word variously translated as Freshwater Sea, Lake of the Hurons, or simply lake, and early maps generally labelled it Lac des Hurons.

More than a thousand wrecks have been recorded in the lake. Le Griffon, built in 1679 and sailed by Robert Cavalier, Sieur de la Salle, is purportedly the first European vessel on the Great Lakes and the first lost. Sent back with a cargo of pelts in late November 1679, she was never seen again, and two wrecks claimed to be hers remain unverified.

The largest city on the lake is Sarnia, with Bay City, Port Huron and Alpena on the American side and Owen Sound, Collingwood and Parry Sound on Georgian Bay. Thunder Bay National Marine Sanctuary, established in 2000, protects 116 of the recorded wrecks.
lake-lucerne: Lake Lucerne is the fourth largest lake in Switzerland. It has an irregular shape, with sharp bends and four arms, and covers 114 km2 at an elevation of 434 m, with a maximum depth of 214 m. The Reuss enters it at Flüelen, in the part called the Urnersee, and leaves it at Lucerne; the Muota, the Engelberger Aa and the Sarner Aa also flow in. Much of the shoreline rises steeply into mountains up to 1,500 m above the lake, among them the Rigi and Pilatus. Its level was stabilised between 1859 and 1860, when a needle dam was built in the Reuss at Lucerne; before that the lake was liable to flooding along its shore.

The lake formed at the end of the last ice age from the meltwater of the Reuss Glacier, which melted between 20,000 and 15,000 BCE. Archaeologists surveying the lake bed between 2019 and 2021 found the remains of a Bronze Age village with artefacts from around 1000 BCE, which showed that the area was settled 2,000 years earlier than historians had thought. The lake was a transport axis at least since the opening of the Gotthard Pass in 1230, and it was the only connection along that route until 1863. A mail coach road across the pass opened in 1830 with its northern end at Flüelen, and the first steamer, the Stadt Luzern, began service in 1837.

Before the 16th century the whole lake was called the Luzerner See, as it still is in English. The name Vierwaldstättersee, the lake of the four forested settlements, is first used in the 16th century. Since the 14th century the Waldstätte had been the confederate allies Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, and the notion of four, with the addition of the canton of Lucerne, is first recorded in the 1450s. The meadow of the Rütli, on the shore of the Urnersee, is the traditional site of the founding of the Swiss Confederation.

Many of the oldest communities of Switzerland lie along the shore, among them Küssnacht, Weggis, Vitznau, Gersau, Brunnen, Altdorf and Buochs. Steamers and other passenger boats still ply between the villages and towns, and the lake remains a popular destination for visitors. The Vitznau-Rigi Railway, opened in 1871, was the first rack railway in Europe, and in 1889 a cog railway was built from Alpnachstad up Pilatus. The 35 km Swiss Path around the Urnersee was built in 1991 for the country's 700th anniversary. Ludwig Rellstab's description of moonlight on the lake in 1832 gave Beethoven's Moonlight Sonata its name.
lake-malawi: Lake Malawi is between 560 and 580 kilometres long and about 75 kilometres wide at its widest point, with a surface area of about 29,600 square kilometres. Its deepest point, in a depression in the north-central part, is 706 metres, while the southern half is shallower. The Shire River drains it at the south into the Zambezi. It is a meromictic lake, which means its water layers do not mix.

The lake lies in a valley formed by the opening of the East African Rift, where the African plate is being split. It was long estimated to be 1 to 2 million years old, but more recent evidence points to a considerably older lake, whose basin began to form about 8.6 million years ago. Its levels have varied dramatically, from almost 600 metres below the present level to 10 to 20 metres above it, and at times the lake nearly dried out. Between 1390 and 1860 it may have stood 120 to 150 metres below its present level.

The Portuguese trader Candido José da Costa Cardoso was the first European to visit the lake, in 1846. David Livingstone reached it in 1859 and named it Lake Nyasa. He also called it the Lake of Stars, after the lights of fishermen's lanterns on the water, and the Lake of Storms, after the violent gales that sweep it.

On 16 August 1914 the lake saw a brief naval battle of the First World War. The British gunboat Gwendolen found the German Empire's only gunboat on the lake, the Hermann von Wissmann, in a bay near Sphinxhaven and disabled it with a single cannon shot from about 1,800 metres. The Times hailed it as the first naval victory of the war for the British Empire.

The lake's borders rest on colonial agreements. In 1954 a British and Portuguese agreement made the middle of the lake the boundary with Mozambique, except for Chizumulu and Likoma islands, now part of Malawi. Between Malawi and Tanzania both sides cite the Heligoland Treaty of 1890, and Tanzania protested officially in 1967.

The lake is known as Lake Malawi, Lake Nyasa in Tanzania and Lago Niassa in Mozambique. It is home to more species of fish than any other lake, including at least 700 species of cichlid. Part of it is included in Lake Malawi National Park at the southern end, and the portion in Mozambique was declared a reserve in 2011.
lake-maracaibo: Lake Maracaibo lies in north-western Venezuela between the states of Zulia, Trujillo and Mérida. Its present hydrology may classify it better as an estuary or semi-enclosed bay connected to the Gulf of Venezuela by a narrow strait. With a surface area of 13,512 square kilometres it would be the largest lake in South America if counted as one, and it is said to be one of the oldest lakes on Earth, formed some 36 million years ago when faults collapsed as the Andes rose in the late Eocene.
It is about 210 kilometres long and 121 wide, and many rivers feed it, the largest being the Catatumbo. Above its southern part occur the almost silent flashes known as Catatumbo lightning.

The Añú people who lived on its banks call it Coquivacoa, and the Wayuu, Caquetíos and Quiriquires also lived in the area. When Amerigo Vespucci and the fleet of Alonso de Ojeda sailed there on 24 August 1499, the stilt houses of the Añú reminded Vespucci of Venice, and he named the region Veneziola, or Little Venice, from which the name Venezuela comes. Spain made two attempts to settle around the lake, in 1529 and 1569, but the city of Maracaibo was successfully founded only in 1574.

The privateer Henry Morgan raided settlements on the lake in the spring of 1669 and defeated a Spanish squadron sent to intercept him. On 24 July 1823 Venezuela won the Battle of Lake Maracaibo during its War of Independence.

The first Spaniards used tar seeping from the lake to caulk ships. The Maracaibo oil field was discovered in 1914, the first well was built in 1917, and large-scale exploitation began in 1922. Dredging in the 1930s deepened the lake's mouth from about 4 to 8 metres, and a breakwater finished in 1957 allowed ocean-going tankers to enter, which turned the northern part from fresh water to brackish.

The lake and the Catatumbo River are main routes for goods in the region, and the city of Maracaibo, capital of Zulia State, is an oil port and a transshipment centre for coffee from the Andes. Fishing families live in traditional stilt houses on the water. The General Rafael Urdaneta Bridge, 8,678 metres long, crosses the strait and was completed in 1962, at its inauguration the longest cable-stayed concrete bridge in the world.
lake-nasser: Lake Nasser is one of the largest man-made lakes in the world. It is named after Gamal Abdel Nasser, the second president of Egypt. Strictly the name applies only to the larger part of the lake, which lies in Egyptian territory and makes up 83 percent of the total; the Sudanese prefer to call their smaller part Lake Nubia. The lake is about 16 km across at its widest point, near the Tropic of Cancer, covers 5,250 square kilometres and holds some 132 cubic kilometres of water. When the water is high enough the overflow empties westward into the Toshka Lakes.

Before the lake, the land it covers was a significant part of Nubia, home to several pharaohs of Egypt and to empires such as that of Kush. Construction of the Aswan High Dam began in 1960 at the wish of Nasser and was finished in 1970; President Anwar Sadat inaugurated the dam and lake in 1971. The dam replaced the insufficient Aswan Low Dam of 1902, and its aims were a more stable water supply, more agricultural production and electricity for Egypt. Sudan opposed the project beforehand because it would flood land in the north of the country where many Nubians lived and would have to be resettled.

Tens of thousands of Nubians were forced to leave their homes, and although some settled on the new shores, their original homes were lost. The flooding of the region also prompted the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia, led by UNESCO. The temples of Kalabsha, Wadi es-Sebua and Amada were saved and moved, and the temples at Abu Simbel were taken apart and rebuilt safely above the lake. Others, such as the fortress of Buhen, could not be rescued and lie under the water.

The lake gives Egypt irrigation water through the year in place of the seasonal floods of the Nile, and the country's arable land increased by about 30 percent. Damming the Nile has cut the supply of nutrients that the floods once brought downstream, so farmers use mineral fertilisers. The lake has 52 species of fish, among them tilapia, which make up most of the catch, and the Nile perch. The Aswan High Dam produces about 2.1 gigawatts of hydroelectricity. Cruises and the relocated monuments, above all Abu Simbel, draw visitors.
lake-tanganyika: Lake Tanganyika is an African Great Lake and the world's longest freshwater lake. It is the second largest freshwater lake by volume and the second deepest, after Lake Baikal. It extends 676 km north to south, covers 32,000 square kilometres and has a mean depth of 572 m and a maximum depth of 1,471 m. It lies in the Albertine Rift and is shared among Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi and Zambia. It is one of only twenty lakes more than a million years old.

The one major outflow, the Lukuga River, runs into the Congo system, and in the past the lake has rarely had an outflow to the sea. Its deeper waters hold no oxygen, which limits fish to the upper layers. It has at least 250 endemic species of cichlid fishes and supports a major fishery.

In the mid-19th century Swahili Arab traders from Zanzibar established a caravan route from Bagamoyo through Tabora to Ujiji on the lake. They brought sailing dhows and traded in slaves, ivory, guns and cotton, and Tippu Tip established a state west of the lake. The British explorers Richard Burton and John Speke, searching for the source of the Nile, were the first known Westerners to reach it, in 1858. David Livingstone visited it several times in 1866-73 and met Henry Morton Stanley at Ujiji in 1871. Britain, Germany and King Leopold of Belgium established colonies on the lake in the late 19th century and in the early 20th ended the slave trade.

During the First World War the Germans, with the ship Graf Goetzen, held complete control of the lake early on. Lieutenant Commander Geoffrey Spicer-Simson of the Royal Navy brought two armed motor boats, HMS Mimi and HMS Toutou, from England by rail, road and river to Albertville, now Kalemie. In December 1915 they captured the gunboat Kingani, and the Hedwig was sunk in February 1916. The Goetzen was scuttled on 26 July 1916, raised in 1924 and renamed MV Liemba.
lake-victoria: Lake Victoria is one of the African Great Lakes. It covers about 59,947 square kilometres and is the world's largest tropical lake and the second-largest fresh water lake by surface area after Lake Superior. It lies in a shallow depression, with an average depth of 40 metres and a maximum of about 80 metres, and its catchment area covers 169,858 square kilometres. Tanzania holds 49 per cent of the lake, Uganda 45 per cent and Kenya 6 per cent.

The lake receives 80 per cent of its water from direct rainfall, the rest from rivers and streams, the largest of which is the Kagera River on the western shore. Its only outflow is the Nile River near Jinja, Uganda. One account puts the lake's age at about 400,000 years: it formed as westward-flowing rivers were backed up when a block of the Earth's crust tilted along the Great Rift Valley. Its shores are home to haplochromine cichlids, of which more than 500 species are almost all found nowhere else.

The first recorded information about the lake comes from Arab traders who travelled the inland routes in search of gold, ivory, other goods and slaves. Many African peoples lived in the catchment area. The explorer John Hanning Speke, travelling with Richard Francis Burton, was the first European to see it, reaching its southern shore in 1858. He named it after Queen Victoria and believed he had found the source of the Nile.

Burton, who was recovering from illness at Kazeh, near present-day Tabora, rejected the claim as unproven. A very public quarrel followed, which provoked debate among scientists and drew other explorers to confirm or refute Speke's view. In 1952 engineers acting for the government of colonial Uganda blasted out the natural rock weir at Jinja, which had controlled the outflow for at least 12,000 years, and replaced it with a barrage. Uganda later added the Kiira Hydroelectric Power Station, completed in 2002.

The lake supports Africa's largest inland fishery. Nile perch and several tilapias were introduced in the 1950s, and the Nile perch in particular is blamed for the extinction of many native cichlids; the loss has been called the most dramatic example of human-caused extinctions within an ecosystem. Kisumu, Kampala, Entebbe, Jinja, Mwanza and Bukoba are among the towns and cities on or near the shore. Ferries have been an important means of transport between Uganda, Tanzania and Kenya since the 1900s, and the main ports are Kisumu, Mwanza, Bukoba, Entebbe, Port Bell and Jinja.
laos: Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia, bordered by Myanmar and China to the north-west, Vietnam to the east, Cambodia to the south-east and Thailand to the west and south-west. Its forested landscape is mostly mountains, the highest being Phou Bia at 2,818 metres. The Mekong forms part of the western boundary with Thailand, the Annamite Range makes up most of the eastern border, and there are two major plateaus, the Xiangkhoang in the north and the Bolaven in the south. The climate is mostly tropical savanna, with a rainy season from May to October.

A skull at least 46,000 years old found in Tam Pa Ling Cave in the Annamite Mountains was the oldest modern human fossil in Southeast Asia at the time of its recovery in 2009. An agricultural society developed during the 4th millennium BCE, bronze artefacts appeared around 1500 BCE and iron tools by 700 BCE. Tai-speaking groups migrated south-west from Guangxi into present-day Laos and Thailand between the 8th and 10th centuries.

Prince Fa Ngum founded the kingdom of Lan Xang, meaning a million elephants, in the 14th century. Leading 10,000 Khmer troops, he conquered principalities in the Mekong basin and captured Vientiane, and he made Theravada Buddhism the state religion. Ministers forced him into exile in 1373. Photisarath moved the capital from Luang Prabang to Vientiane in 1520 to counter the threat of a Burmese invasion, and Setthathirath, who became king in 1548, commissioned That Luang. Sourigna Vongsa expanded the borders after 1637, and when he died without an heir the kingdom split in 1707 into Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Champasak.

Anouvong, installed by the Siamese as vassal king of Vientiane, launched an unsuccessful rebellion against Siam in 1826 under Vietnamese pressure; Vientiane was ransacked and he died a captive in Bangkok. The three kingdoms were unified under French rule in 1893 as part of French Indochina. Laos regained full independence in 1953 as a constitutional monarchy under Sisavang Vong. A civil war from 1959 to 1975 pitted the communist Pathet Lao against the Royal Lao Armed Forces, backed by the United States, and ended with the founding of the Lao People's Democratic Republic in 1975.

Laos is a unitary communist state led by the Lao People's Revolutionary Party. More than half the population is ethnic Lao, and 66 per cent were Theravada Buddhist in 2010. The country has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Luang Prabang, Vat Phou and the Plain of Jars.
latin: Latin is a classical language of the Italic branch of the Indo-European languages, originally spoken by the Latins in Latium, the lower Tiber area around Rome. Through the expansion of the Roman Republic it became the dominant language of the Italian Peninsula and then of the Roman Empire. The earliest known form, Old Latin, was spoken from the Roman Kingdom, traditionally founded in 753 BCE, through the later Republic until 75 BCE. It is attested in inscriptions and in some of the earliest surviving literary works, such as the comedies of Plautus and Terence. The Latin alphabet was devised from the Etruscan alphabet, which was drawn from the Greek, and the writing changed from a right-to-left or boustrophedon script to a strictly left-to-right one.

From about 75 BCE to 200 CE a new Classical Latin arose, a conscious creation of the orators, poets, historians and other literate men who wrote the great works of classical literature, which were taught in grammar and rhetoric schools. Beside it stood the informal registers called Vulgar Latin, a term Cicero's sermo vulgi renders as the speech of the masses, found in Plautus and in fragments of everyday speech. Late Latin is the literary form from the 3rd century CE onward.

Latin grammar is highly fusional: nouns and adjectives belong to one of five declensions and have seven cases, and verbs are inflected for person, number, tense, voice, mood and aspect. Word order is relatively free because inflections show the connections between words. After the fall of Tarentum in 272 BCE the Romans began Hellenising, borrowing Greek words and adding the letters Y and Z to the alphabet. Classical Latin had no punctuation, letter case or word spacing, and ancient numbers were written only with letters.

Between the 6th and 9th centuries natural change in the vernacular Latin of different regions evolved into distinct Romance languages, among them Italian, French, Portuguese, Spanish, Romanian, Catalan, Romansh and Sardinian. Although often called a dead language, Latin did not undergo language death as formally defined. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire it remained the common language of international communication, science and scholarship in Europe into the early 19th century.

Medieval Latin served as a working and literary language across Western and Catholic Europe from the 9th century to the Renaissance, which then developed Renaissance Latin, the basis of Neo-Latin. It was taught to be written and spoken at least until the late seventeenth century. Latin roots appear in the technical vocabulary of theology, the sciences, medicine and law. About 270,000 Latin inscriptions are known, and Ecclesiastical Latin remains the official language of the Holy See.
latin-america: Latin America is defined by culture rather than geography: it is the part of the Americas where Spanish or Portuguese is the national language, with a common culture and tradition, and where the dominant religion is Roman Catholic. It therefore includes countries from both North and South America, most of Central America, South America and the Caribbean. English-speaking and Dutch-speaking countries such as Belize, Guyana and Suriname are not counted, because they speak Germanic languages. Hispanic America is the narrower term for the Spanish-speaking nations, and Ibero-America the broader one. Most of the region lies in the Neotropical realm, which holds more tropical rainforest than any other, including the Amazon.

Before Europeans arrived in the late 15th and early 16th centuries the region was home to many indigenous peoples, including the Olmec, Maya, Muisca, Aztecs and Inca. The kingdoms of Spain and Portugal established colonies, imposed Roman Catholicism and their languages, and brought African slaves as labourers. The Spanish Crown allowed only Christians to emigrate to the New World, and until independence trade was regulated by the Casa de Contratación in Seville. The term Latin America was first used in 1856 at a conference in Paris, where the Chilean politician Francisco Bilbao used it for countries sharing a cultural and linguistic heritage, and it gained prominence in the 1860s under Napoleon III, whose government sought to justify French intervention in the Second Mexican Empire.

In the early 19th century nearly all of Spanish America won independence by armed struggle, the exceptions being Cuba and Puerto Rico. Brazil became a monarchy separate from Portugal and a republic in the late 19th century. Independence did not end black slavery, and it brought political and economic instability. As regional caudillos rose, leaders shifted from aristocracy toward republicanism. Great Britain and the United States exercised considerable power in the economic sphere while the new nations kept political sovereignty, a situation described as neo-colonialism. Puerto Rico passed to the United States after the Spanish-American War of 1898.

Spanish is spoken as a first language by about 60 per cent of the population and Portuguese by about 30 per cent, mostly in Brazil, the largest and most populous country. About 10 per cent speak other languages such as Quechua, Mayan languages, Guaraní, Aymara and Nahuatl. Most people are Christians, mostly Roman Catholics, and the population descends from indigenous peoples, Europeans, Africans and Asians. Indigenous languages left loanwords in Spanish and Portuguese such as pampa, taco and cacique, and the Maya, Aztecs and Inca are among the indigenous civilizations whose legacies remain strong.
lau-islands: The Lau Islands, also called the Lau Group or the Eastern Group, lie in the southern Pacific just east of the Koro Sea. About thirty of the islands and islets are inhabited. The group has a land area of 487 square kilometres and had a population of 10,683 at the census of 2007. Most of the northern islands are high and of volcanic origin, while those of the south are mostly low carbonate islands.

The islands lie between Melanesian Fiji and Polynesian Tonga and are a meeting point of the two cultural spheres. The south-east trade winds made it easy to sail from Tonga to Fiji and much harder to return. The culture of the islands became more Fijian than Polynesian from around 500 BCE, but Tongan influence remains in names, language, food and architecture: Lauan houses tend to have rounded ends, as in Tonga, where most Fijian houses are square-ended.

The British explorer James Cook reached Vatoa in 1774, and by 1820, when the Ono Group was sighted by Europeans, Lau was the most thoroughly mapped part of Fiji. The first missionaries arrived at Lakeba in 1830 but were expelled.

Political unity came late. The islands formed three territories. Northern Lau, as far south as Tuvuca, was under the overlordship of Taveuni and paid tribute to the Tui Cakau, paramount chief of Cakaudrove. Southern Lau, from Ono-i-Lau north to Cicia, was the traditional chiefdom of the Tui Nayau. The Moala Islands were closer to Bau Island and Lomaiviti. Around 1855 Enele Ma'afu, with the help of the Tui Nayau's army, conquered the region and set up a single administration, with Lomaloma on Vanua Balavu as his capital. The Tui Nayau gave him the title Tui Lau, King of Lau.

The title Tui Lau was vacant after the death of Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna in 1958. In 1963 the Vuanirewa clan bestowed it on Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara, who was also installed as Tui Nayau after his father, Ratu Tevita Uluilakeba II, died in 1966, so that the two titles came into personal union in 1969.

Lauan villages remain very traditional, and the islanders are known for wood carving and masi painting. Cricket, not rugby or football, is the most popular team sport, and Lauan players dominate Fiji's national cricket team. In July 2014 Tonga's lands minister, Lord Maʻafu Tukuiʻaulahi, proposed that Tonga give the disputed Minerva Reefs to Fiji in exchange for the Lau Group; the proposal had not then been discussed with the Lau Provincial Council.
lausanne: Lausanne is a hilly city on the shores of Lake Geneva, about halfway between the Jura Mountains and the Alps, and it faces the French town of Évian-les-Bains across the water. It is built on the southern slope of the Swiss Plateau, with a difference in elevation of about 500 metres between the lakeshore at Ouchy and its northern edge. The city looks out over the lake and the Swiss and Savoyan Alps. Geneva, the nearest major city, lies 51.7 kilometres to the south-west.

The Romans built a military camp, which they called Lousanna, at the site of a Celtic settlement near the lake, where Vidy and Ouchy are situated. On the hill above stood a fort called Lausodunon or Lousodunon. By the 2nd century CE the place was known as vikanor[um] Lousonnensium, and by 400 as civitas Lausanna. The town later grew up at the foot of the cathedral of Notre Dame.

Forces from the canton of Bern invaded in 1536, and Bern ruled Lausanne until 1798. The Bernese stripped the cathedral of its Roman Catholic furnishings and removed a number of its treasures, including its hanging tapestries, which were never returned despite repeated requests from the city. The period brought mixed fortunes, but trade grew, municipal wealth increased and so did landownership, and influential patrician families rose, among them the Loys, the Seigneux, the de Praroman and the de Saussure.

On 24 July 1923 the Treaty of Lausanne, which established the modern Turkish Republic, was signed at the Beau-Rivage Palace. Lausanne hosted the Swiss National Exhibition in 1964. From the 1950s to the 1970s many Italians, Spaniards and Portuguese settled there, mostly in the industrial suburb of Renens.

Lausanne is the capital and largest city of the French-speaking canton of Vaud, with a municipal population of about 150,000. The Federal Supreme Court of Switzerland convenes there, although the city is not the nation's capital. It has been recognised as the Olympic Capital since 1994, and it hosts the International Olympic Committee, the Court of Arbitration for Sport and some 55 international sport associations. Its 28-station metro makes it the smallest city in the world with a rapid transit system.

Since the Reformation the city was mostly Protestant until the late 20th century, when immigration from largely Catholic countries made Catholics the largest group. The whole old city is listed in the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites, and the cathedral, restored by Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, and Saint-Maire Castle are among its main monuments. Its universities include the University of Lausanne and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne.
lazio: Lazio borders Tuscany, Umbria and Marche to the north, Abruzzo and Molise to the east, Campania to the south and the Tyrrhenian Sea to the west. The region is mainly hilly and mountainous, with plains along the coast and the Tiber valley. The Roman Campagna, a vast alluvial plain, surrounds Rome, and in the south the Agro Pontino was once a swampy and malarial area that was reclaimed over the centuries. Volcanic groups such as the Volsini, Cimini and Sabatini hold lakes in their old craters, among them Bolsena, Vico and Bracciano.

Latium was the region of the Latins, whose city-state became Rome. In remote antiquity it covered only a small part of the present region, between the lower Tiber, the Tyrrhenian Sea, the Monti Sabini and the Pontine Marshes. The land the Latins held later extended into the territory of the Samnites, the Marsi, the Hernici, the Aequi, the Aurunci and the Volsci, and was divided into Latium Vetus, Old Latium, and Latium adiectum, the added lands. The Tiber separated it from Etruria.

After the Gothic conquest of Italy at the end of the fifth century, the region belonged to the Ostrogothic Kingdom. Following the Gothic War of 535 to 554 it became the property of the Eastern Emperor as the Duchy of Rome. The Donation of Sutri in 728 gave the Pope his first territory in the region beyond the Duchy of Rome. Secular lords and the popes struggled for power until the middle of the 16th century, and the lords gained strength while the papacy resided at Avignon from 1309 to 1377. From the middle of the 16th century the papacy unified Lazio politically with the Papal States.

Lazio returned to the Papal States in October 1799 after the short-lived Roman Republic, was annexed to the French Empire in 1809, and returned to the Pope in 1815. On 20 September 1870 Rome was captured, and Lazio was incorporated into the Kingdom of Italy. In 1927 the province of Rieti joined it.

Lazio is one of the 20 administrative regions of Italy, with Rome as its capital and as the capital of Italy. It is the second most populated region, with more than five million inhabitants. Among its sights are the Roman Castles around the Alban Hills, the archaeological park of Ostia Antica, the port of ancient Rome, and the abbeys of Monte Cassino and Farfa.
le-corbusier: Charles-Édouard Jeanneret was born on 6 October 1887 in La Chaux-de-Fonds, in the canton of Neuchâtel in French-speaking Switzerland. His father was an artisan who enamelled boxes and watches, and his mother taught piano. His ancestors included Belgians with the surname Lecorbésier, which inspired the pseudonym Le Corbusier. He acquired French nationality in 1930.

In 1905, with two other students and under the supervision of their teacher René Chapallaz, he designed and built his first house, the Villa Fallet, a large chalet in the local alpine style. He first discovered reinforced concrete while working in the office of Auguste Perret in Paris, and in December 1914 he began a serious study of it as a building material.

Le Corbusier moved to Paris definitively in 1917 and began an architectural practice with his cousin Pierre Jeanneret. In 1918 he met the painter Amédée Ozenfant, and together they rejected Cubism and founded the movement Purism. Their journal L'Esprit Nouveau carried his polemical articles, which he collected in 1923 as his first and most influential book, Towards an Architecture. His book The Decorative Art of Today (1925) attacked the idea of decorative art itself.

In 1927 he published, with Pierre Jeanneret, the Five Points of a Modern Architecture, which include raising the building on reinforced concrete pilotis and replacing the sloping roof with a roof terrace. He put them into practice most dramatically in the Villa Savoye, built from 1928 to 1931. In 1926 his project for the League of Nations headquarters in Geneva appeared to be the jury's first choice among 337 entries, but the commission went instead to five neoclassical architects. He was a founding member of the Congrès Internationaux d'Architecture Moderne in 1928 and prepared the master plan for Chandigarh in India.

Le Corbusier died of a heart attack while swimming at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin on 27 August 1965. In 1959 a campaign had saved the Villa Savoye from demolition by having it declared a historic monument, the first such distinction for a work by a living architect. In 2016 seventeen of his projects in seven countries were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list. He remains a controversial figure: his ties with fascism, antisemitism and Benito Mussolini continue to be debated, and some of his urban planning ideas have been criticised for their indifference to existing cultural sites.
league-of-nations: Immanuel Kant's Perpetual Peace of 1795 had outlined the idea of a league of nations, and the Concert of Europe after the Napoleonic Wars was an early attempt at collective security. Schemes for an international organisation gained public support in the First World War. The British political scientist Goldsworthy Lowes Dickinson coined the term League of Nations in 1914. At the Paris Peace Conference in 1919 Woodrow Wilson, Cecil and Smuts all put forward drafts, and the delegates approved the creation of the League on 25 January 1919. The Covenant was signed on 28 April 1919 as Part I of the Treaty of Versailles and took effect on 10 January 1920.

The League lacked an armed force and depended on the victorious Allied Powers to enforce its resolutions and sanctions, which they were often reluctant to do. The League had 42 founding members in November 1920 and 58 at its largest, between 28 September 1934 and 23 February 1935. The United States never joined, and Germany and Japan left in 1933. The Soviet Union joined only in 1934 and was expelled in 1939 after invading Finland. Italy left in 1937. In 1921 it fixed Albania's frontiers as those of 1913, with three minor changes that favoured Yugoslavia.

The League supervised the mandates, which took in the former German colonies and Arabic-speaking Ottoman provinces. Fourteen mandate territories were divided among seven mandatory powers: the United Kingdom, South Africa, France, Belgium, New Zealand, Australia and Japan. During the Second Italo-Ethiopian War, Benito Mussolini answered the League's accusations by saying that it was very well when sparrows shout but no good when eagles fall out. The outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 showed that it had failed its main purpose, and it was largely inactive until it ceased operations on 18 April 1946.

The League had several wings and agencies: the Permanent Court of International Justice, the International Labour Organization, the Health Organisation, the Mandates Commission, the Slavery Commission. Three of them passed to the United Nations after the Second World War: the Labour Organization, the Court, as the International Court of Justice, and the Health Organisation, as the World Health Organization. Scholars now generally hold that although the League failed to secure world peace, it extended the rule of law, strengthened collective security and gave a voice to smaller nations. Its mandate system also put colonial powers under international observation.
lebanon: Lebanon lies in the Levant between latitudes 33° and 35° N, bordered by Syria to the north and east, Israel to the south and the Mediterranean Sea to the west. Its area is 10,452 square kilometres. The country has four physiographic regions: a narrow coastal plain, the Lebanon mountain range, the Beqaa Valley and the Anti-Lebanon Mountains. The Lebanon range peaks at 3,088 metres in Qurnat as Sawda', while the Beqaa, part of the Great Rift Valley system, is 180 kilometres long. The longest river, the Leontes, is 145 kilometres long and empties into the Mediterranean north of Tyre.

Byblos, among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, shows settlement earlier than 5000 BCE. Lebanon was part of northern Canaan and the homeland of the Phoenicians, whose most prominent cities were Byblos, Sidon and Tyre. The Phoenicians are credited with the oldest verified alphabet.

Foreign powers, beginning with the Neo-Assyrian Empire, imposed tribute; the cities passed to the Neo-Babylonian Empire and in 539 BCE to the Achaemenid Empire, and later to Alexander the Great after the siege of Tyre in 332 BCE. Pompey annexed Syria in 64 BCE. In the late 4th and early 5th century a hermit named Maron founded a monastic tradition whose followers, the Maronites, moved into the mountains.

After the seventh century the region came under Arab caliphates, then Crusader states, the Ayyubids and the Mamluks, and in the early 16th century Ottoman rule. The Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate was set up under Sultan Abdulmejid I as a home for Maronite Christians. France administered the Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon after the First World War and created Greater Lebanon in 1920; independence came by 1943. The Lebanese Civil War lasted from 1975 to 1990, and Syria occupied the country from 1976 to 2005 and Israel from 1982 to 2000.

The National Pact of 1943 apportions power among the religious groups: the president is a Maronite Christian, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim and the speaker of Parliament a Shi'a Muslim. The 128 seats of Parliament are divided equally between Christians and Muslims, a balance fixed by the Taif Agreement that ended the civil war. No official census has been held since 1932 because of the sensitivity of the confessional balance. More Lebanese, counting partial ancestry, live abroad than in the country, with the largest community in Brazil.
lee-kuan-yew: Lee Kuan Yew was born Harry Lee Kuan Yew on 16 September 1923 in Singapore, then part of the Straits Settlements, the first child of Lee Chin Koon and Chua Jim Neo, both English-educated third-generation Peranakan Chinese. During the Japanese occupation he was among the Chinese men rounded up in the Sook Ching operation and left the screening site on the second day, later learning that the group of men was likely taken to the beach and executed. In 1946 he sailed for the United Kingdom, studied law at Cambridge, and returned to Singapore in 1950. In London he had met Goh Keng Swee and Toh Chin Chye, and after his return they formed a political party.

Lee co-founded the People's Action Party (PAP) in 1954, and after it won the 1959 election he became prime minister. He and his colleagues held that Singapore could survive only through merger with Malaya. On 16 September 1963 he proclaimed Singapore part of Malaysia, together with Sabah and Sarawak, and tensions with the federal government over industrialisation and taxes followed; Singapore became independent in 1965.

As prime minister of the new state he appointed Goh Keng Swee to build the armed forces, introduced conscription in 1967, addressed unemployment through manufacturing, and gave the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau greater powers. Critics have described his government as an illiberal democracy that restricted press freedom and public assembly, and from 1968 to 1981 Singapore was a de facto one-party state.
He stepped down on 28 November 1990 after seven election victories, handing the premiership to Goh Chok Tong, and remained in the Cabinet as Senior Minister until 2004 and Minister Mentor until 2011.

Lee died of pneumonia on 23 March 2015, aged 91. A week of national mourning was announced, during which approximately 1.7 million people paid their respects. In Singapore he is widely regarded as instrumental in the development of the economy, education system, public housing and healthcare, and the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy at the National University of Singapore bears his name. He argued that communitarianism and limited human rights were necessary for rapid economic development, and he said that he had had to do some nasty things, locking fellows up without trial.
legio-xii-fulminata: The legion was levied by Julius Caesar in 58 BCE and accompanied him through the Gallic Wars until 49 BCE. It fought in the battle against the Nervians and probably at the Siege of Alesia, and was at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE, when Caesar defeated Pompey. After the civil war it was named Victrix; in 43 BCE it was enlisted by Lepidus and Mark Antony, who led it, renamed XII Antiqua, on his campaign against the Parthian Empire. In the later part of the reign of Augustus it served in Syria, camped at Raphana.

In 62 CE the Twelfth joined Legio IV Scythica under Lucius Caesennius Paetus and both were defeated by the Parthians and Armenians at the battle of Rhandeia; after their surrender the legions were shamed and withdrawn from that theatre. In 66, sent with detachments of two other legions to restore Roman authority in Jerusalem, it was ambushed by Eleazar ben Simon at the Battle of Beth Horon during the withdrawal of Cestius Gallus and lost its eagle. It fought well in the later part of the First Jewish–Roman War and supported Vespasian's bid for the throne, after which it was posted to Melitene with Legio XVI Flavia Firma.

In 75 Vespasian sent it to the Caucasus to support the allied kingdoms of Iberia and Albania. It was probably in Armenia for Trajan's campaign of 114, and in 134 helped the governor Arrian defeat the Alans. Under Marcus Aurelius it campaigned against the Quadi, where the sources report a rain and lightning storm, held to be miraculous, that saved one of its units; a belief that the emperor then forbade the persecution of Christians seems to rest on a forgery. Its loyalty during the revolt of Avidius Cassius in 175 earned the title Certa Constans, surely constant.

After the death of Pertinax in 193 the legion backed Pescennius Niger against Septimius Severus, and when the frontier was moved from the Euphrates to the Tigris it stayed in reserve, possibly as a punishment. The country around Melitene was among the first where Christianity spread, and Polyeuctes, a martyr under Valerian, was a soldier of the Twelfth. In the 3rd century it was under the command of Odaenathus of Palmyra, yet also received the title Galliena from Emperor Gallienus. Records then become scarce. The Notitia Dignitatum still lists it guarding the Euphrates at Melitene at the beginning of the 5th century.
leicester: Leicester stands on the River Soar, about 90 miles north-north-west of London, and is the county town of Leicestershire. Its name comes from Old English. It is first recorded in Latinised form in the early ninth century, appears as Ligera ceastre in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 924 and as Ledecestre in the Domesday Book of 1086.

The Iron Age settlement that the Romans met seems to have developed in the 2nd or 1st century BCE, with roundhouses along the east bank of the Soar and control of a ford. The tribe that held the area were the Corieltauvians. The Romans arrived around 47 CE, and from about 50 the settlement near a bridge on the Fosse Way developed as the tribal capital under the name Ratae Corieltauvorum. In the 2nd century it received a forum and a bathhouse, whose remains can be seen at the Jewry Wall.

After the Roman withdrawal the town seems to have been continuously occupied, with a much reduced population, and its memory was kept as Cair Lerion in the History of the Britons. It was occupied by the Middle Angles and then administered by Mercia, and it became a bishopric in 679 or 680. The see lasted until the 9th century, when Danish Vikings captured the town, and the settlement became one of the Five Burghs of the Danelaw. Leicester became a bishopric again only in 1927, when the parish church of St Martin became its cathedral.

After the Norman Conquest the town came under the Beaumont and De Montfort earls, notably Simon de Montfort, and after his death in 1265 it passed to the House of Lancaster, for whom Leicester Castle was a stronghold and, from 1399, a royal residence. Parliaments met there in 1318, 1414 and 1450. In the Early Modern era Puritanism flourished and the town supported the Parliamentarian cause in the Civil War. In the Victorian age it became known for hosiery and shoe manufacturing, and it gained city status in 1919.

Leicester is the largest city in the East Midlands, with a population of 383,116. Since the middle of the 20th century immigration from countries of the British Commonwealth has made it ethnically diverse. King Richard III spent his last days in the town before his death at the Battle of Bosworth and was buried there in August 1485; he was reburied in Leicester Cathedral in 2015, after his remains were found nearby in the foundations of the lost Greyfriars chapel.
leipzig: Leipzig lies in the Leipzig Bay, the southernmost part of the North German Plain, about 150 km south-west of Berlin. The White Elster is joined there by the Pleiße and the Parthe, and the three rivers form a broad delta-like landscape of swampy ground, known as the Leipziger Gewässerknoten. The Via Regia and the Via Imperii, two important medieval trade routes, crossed at the site, which marked the city's economic importance. The name is commonly held to derive from the Slavic word lipa, linden tree, which gave the city the poetic epithet Lindenstadt, though more recent research on the oldest forms of the name has questioned this.

Leipzig was first documented in 1015 in the chronicle of Bishop Thietmar of Merseburg as urbs Libzi, and received city and market privileges in 1165 from Otto the Rich. Its trade fair dates back to 1190 and is the oldest surviving trade fair in the world, which encouraged the growth of a merchant bourgeoisie. Between 1764 and 1945 the city was a centre of publishing. The Battle of the Nations of 1813 was the largest battle in Europe before the First World War, and the Monument to the Battle of the Nations marking its centenary was completed in 1913. Although over half of the Kingdom of Saxony was ceded to Prussia, Leipzig stayed with King Frederick Augustus I.

By 1907 the Leipziger Baumwollspinnerei, with over 240,000 spindles, was the largest cotton mill company on the continent. The population peaked at over 700,000 in 1930, fell to about 530,000 by 1989 and to 437,000 by 1998, mostly through outward migration and suburbanisation, and then rose again after the city area was almost doubled by the incorporation of surrounding towns in 1999.

Leipzig is the most populous city in the German state of Saxony, with about 620,000 inhabitants, and part of the Central German Metropolitan Region. It is a long-standing centre of music: the Thomanerchor was founded in 1212, the Gewandhaus Orchestra in 1743 and the Oper Leipzig in 1693, and Felix Mendelssohn established Germany's first musical conservatoire there in 1843. Richard Wagner was born in the city in 1813. The Leipzig Hauptbahnhof, opened in 1915, is the largest overhead railway station in Europe by built-up area. Leipzig is also the main seat of the German National Library.
leo-tolstoy: Tolstoy was born on 9 September 1828 (28 August in the Old Style calendar) at Yasnaya Polyana, a family estate 12 kilometres southwest of Tula. He was the fourth of five children of Count Nikolai Ilyich Tolstoy, a veteran of the Patriotic War of 1812, and Princess Mariya Volkonskaya. His mother died when he was two and his father when he was nine, and relatives brought up the children. In 1844 he began studying law and oriental languages at Kazan University, where teachers described him as unable and unwilling to learn. He left before finishing and led a lax and leisurely life in Moscow, Tula and Saint Petersburg.

After running up heavy gambling debts, Tolstoy went to the Caucasus with his older brother in 1851 and joined the army. His first novel, Childhood, a fictional account of his own youth, was published in 1852. He served as an artillery officer in the Crimean War and was in Sevastopol during the 11-month siege of 1854–55. Appalled by the number of deaths, he left the army after the war.

Two trips around Europe, in 1857 and 1860–61, converted him from a dissolute society author to a non-violent and spiritual anarchist. In Paris in 1857 he witnessed a public execution, which marked the rest of his life. On 23 September 1862 he married Sophia Andreevna Behrs, sixteen years his junior; they had 13 children, eight of whom survived childhood. She acted as his secretary and editor while he composed War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

His autobiographical trilogy Childhood, Boyhood and Youth (1852–1856) tells of a rich landowner's son who slowly realises the gap between himself and his peasants. Anna Karenina tells parallel stories of an adulterous woman trapped by the conventions of society and of a landowner much like Tolstoy who works alongside peasants. He drew characters in his own image, such as Pierre Bezukhov in War and Peace and Levin in Anna Karenina.

In the 1870s Tolstoy underwent a moral crisis and a spiritual awakening, set out in Confession (1882). A literal reading of Jesus's ethical teaching, centred on the Sermon on the Mount, made him a Christian anarchist and pacifist. His ideas on nonviolent resistance, in works such as The Kingdom of God Is Within You (1894), influenced Mahatma Gandhi, who corresponded with him. He died of pneumonia on 20 November 1910 at Astapovo railway station.
leon-trotsky: Lev Davidovich Bronstein was born on 7 November 1879 in Yanovka, in Kherson Governorate of the Russian Empire, now part of Ukraine, the fifth child of a wealthy but illiterate Jewish farming family. His father intended him to become a mechanical engineer. In 1896 he moved to Nikolayev and became involved in revolutionary activity; at first a narodnik who opposed Marxism, he was converted by his future first wife, Aleksandra Sokolovskaya. He joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in 1898 and was arrested and exiled to Siberia. After escaping in 1902 he went to London, joined Lenin and the other editors of Iskra, and took the name Trotsky. In the 1905 Revolution he was elected chairman of the Saint Petersburg Soviet.

After the February Revolution of 1917 he joined the Bolsheviks and became chairman of the Petrograd Soviet. He helped lead the October Revolution, then as People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs negotiated the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, by which Russia left the First World War. In March 1918 he became People's Commissar of Army and Navy Affairs, with full control of the Red Army. Other Bolshevik military leaders protested against his reliance on strict discipline and former imperial officers. He led the Red Army to victory in the civil war.

As Lenin's health failed, Stalin became General Secretary in 1922, and Zinoviev and Kamenev joined him in a triumvirate to stop Trotsky from succeeding Lenin. From 1923 Trotsky led the Left Opposition. He was expelled from the Politburo in 1926 and from the party in 1927, exiled to Alma Ata in 1928 and expelled from the Soviet Union to Turkey in February 1929. He later lived in France and Norway before settling in Mexico in 1937.

In exile Trotsky wrote against Stalinism, argued in The Revolution Betrayed that the Soviet Union had become a degenerated workers' state, and in 1938 founded the Fourth International. The Moscow show trial of August 1936 sentenced him to death in absentia, and an independent commission chaired by John Dewey found him not guilty of the charges.
