Ramón Mercader, a Stalinist agent, assassinated him in Mexico City, and he died on 21 August 1940. He was written out of official Soviet history and, unlike most of Stalin's rivals, was never rehabilitated by later Soviet leaders. His ideas inspired a school of Marxism known as Trotskyism.
leonardo-da-vinci: Leonardo di ser Piero da Vinci was born on 15 April 1452 in or close to the Tuscan hill town of Vinci, about 35 kilometres from Florence. He was born out of wedlock to Caterina di Meo Lippi, from the lower class, and Piero da Vinci, a Florentine legal notary and landowner. Where he was born is uncertain: a local oral tradition names Anchiano, a hamlet that would have offered privacy, though he may have been born in a house Ser Piero had in Florence.

Both parents married separately the year after his birth, and Leonardo eventually had 16 half-siblings, with whom he had very little contact. He was educated in Florence by Andrea del Verrocchio, under whom he studied anatomy and first gained attention for the Baptism of Christ, painted in conjunction with Verrocchio.

For the better part of four hundred years Leonardo's fame rested on his painting. The qualities of his work include innovative techniques for laying on paint, detailed knowledge of anatomy, light, botany and geology, an interest in how people show emotion in expression and gesture, and subtle gradation of tone. They come together in the Mona Lisa, the Last Supper and the Virgin of the Rocks. He also drew prolifically, producing the Vitruvian Man, a study of the proportions of the human body.

His studies in science and engineering were recorded in about 13,000 pages of notes and drawings that fuse art and natural philosophy. His approach was observational: he tried to understand a phenomenon by describing and depicting it in utmost detail. He lacked formal education in Latin and mathematics, though he taught himself Latin. Relatively few of his designs for flying machines and the like were feasible in his lifetime, and he did not publish his findings.

Leonardo spent his last three years in France at the invitation of Francis I, and was buried in the collegiate church of Saint Florentin at the Château d'Amboise on 12 August 1519. His notebooks passed to his pupil and heir Francesco Melzi, and after Melzi's death in 1570 they were gradually dispersed. Many historians regard Leonardo as the prime exemplar of the Renaissance man or universal genius. The church was demolished in 1802, and the location of his remains is disputed.
leonhard-euler: Leonhard Euler was born in Basel on 15 April 1707, the oldest of four children of Paul III Euler, a pastor of the Reformed Church, and Marguerite, née Brucker. Soon after his birth the family moved to Riehen, where his father became pastor and Euler spent most of his childhood. His father, who had taken courses from Jacob Bernoulli at the University of Basel, taught him mathematics. Around the age of eight he went to live with his maternal grandmother and enrolled at the Latin school in Basel, and he was also tutored privately by the theologian Johannes Burckhardt.

Daniel Bernoulli, who had entered the Imperial Russian Academy of Sciences in Saint Petersburg, recommended Euler for a post, and Euler arrived there in May 1727. He was soon promoted from the medical department to the mathematics department, lodged with Bernoulli, mastered Russian and worked as a medic in the Russian Navy. In June 1741, concerned about turmoil in Russia, he left for the Berlin Academy at the invitation of Frederick the Great of Prussia and lived in Berlin for 25 years. There he published the Introductio in analysin infinitorum in 1748 and the Institutiones calculi differentialis in 1755. In 1766 he accepted an invitation to return to Saint Petersburg after Catherine the Great came to the throne.

Euler married Katharina Gsell on 7 January 1734; of their 13 children, five survived childhood. After her death in 1773 he married her half-sister, Salome Abigail Gsell. He became almost blind in his right eye in 1738, and a cataract in his left was discovered in 1766 and left him almost totally blind. With the help of scribes his productivity in many areas increased; in 1775 he produced on average one mathematical paper a week.

His writings, collected as the Opera Omnia, include 866 publications and over 4,500 letters. Euler introduced or popularised much modern notation, including f(x) for a function, e for the base of the natural logarithm, the Greek letter sigma for summations and i for the imaginary unit, and he popularised the use of the Greek letter pi, which originated with the Welsh mathematician William Jones. In 1735 he solved the Basel problem, finding the sum of the reciprocals of the squares, posed by Pietro Mengoli in 1644.

His solution of the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem, showing that no path crosses each bridge exactly once, is considered the first theorem of graph theory. He also found the formula relating the vertices, edges and faces of a convex polyhedron. Euler died in Saint Petersburg on 18 September 1783 of a brain haemorrhage, after discussing the newly discovered planet Uranus with Anders Johan Lexell. He was buried beside Katharina at the Smolensk Lutheran Cemetery.
leonid-brezhnev: Leonid Ilyich Brezhnev was born on 19 December 1906 in Kamenskoye, in the Yekaterinoslav Governorate of the Russian Empire, now Kamianske in Ukraine, the son of a metalworker. His ethnicity was given as Ukrainian in some documents, including his passport, and as Russian in others. He joined the Communist youth league in 1923 and became a party member in 1929. After the German invasion in June 1941 he oversaw mobilisation and the evacuation of factories, then joined the Red Army as a commissar, serving under Nikita Khrushchev on the Southern Front. He ended the war as a major general.

After the war Brezhnev was first secretary of the Zaporizhzhia and then the Dnipropetrovsk regional party committees. In 1950 he was sent to Moldavia, where he completed the introduction of collective agriculture. In 1955 he became first secretary in Kazakhstan, where he oversaw the construction of the Baikonur Cosmodrome and the Virgin Lands campaign. He joined the Central Committee in 1952 and the Politburo by 1957. Brezhnev stayed outwardly loyal to Khrushchev but became involved in a 1963 plot to remove him. After Khrushchev fell in 1964 he governed at first in a triumvirate with Alexei Kosygin and Nikolai Podgorny.

Brezhnev reached decisions in the Politburo by consensus, restoring the semblance of collective leadership. His rule was associated with the doctrine of Developed Socialism, adopted by him in 1971 and written into the constitution in 1977. In 1968 he publicly denounced the Prague Spring as revisionist, though archives suggest he first sought a compromise before deciding to intervene. Repression and censorship increased compared with the Khrushchev Thaw, and the period became known as the Era of Stagnation, with corruption, fewer consumer goods and slower growth.

A personality cult grew while his health declined. He received over 100 medals and the rank of Marshal of the Soviet Union on his 70th birthday. After a heart attack in 1975 he deferred increasingly to Yuri Andropov, Andrei Gromyko and the defence minister. He died on 10 November 1982, and Andropov succeeded him.
lex-hortensia: In the annalistic tradition a plebeian named Hortensius was appointed dictator around 287 BCE to deal with a civil uprising, which led to the secession of the plebs to the Janiculum hill; they returned only after the law had been passed in the Centuriate Assembly. The annals put the uprising down to debt, with a call to arms against the Lucanians as the immediate occasion, since the patricians needed plebeian manpower for the war.

There is considerable reason to doubt this account, which Livy attributes to an urban rabble in the forum. Large masses of urban poor did not really exist in the middle Republic, and rural landowners controlled 29 of the voting blocs of the Plebeian Council, which never numbered more than 35. The more likely cause is the wish of rural plebeians to control the distribution of the public lands won in the Third Samnite War, though the extreme measures of the consuls suggest considerable unrest in the city as well. An organised movement was needed to pass such a law, and it was probably coordinated by the plebeian tribunes.

In the early Republic the resolutions of the Plebeian Council, the plebiscita, bound only plebeians, because only plebeians voted there. The lex Valeria-Horatia of 449 BCE allowed them to bind all Romans if the Senate ratified them, and the lex Publilia of 339 BCE moved the Senate's approval to before the vote. The Hortensian law removed the requirement altogether. A plebiscitum remained distinct in name from a lex but was now treated as if it were one; later all binding laws came to be called leges.

The law also restricted when votes could be held. They were no longer allowed on market days, when they could have interfered with business, which hindered rural plebeians from taking part, since those were the days when they would have been in the city.

The law secured theoretically equal political rights for patricians and plebeians. It established the pre-eminence of the Tribal Assembly and the Plebeian Council in legislation, so that in the late Republic the other assemblies passed mainly minor and procedural laws, and it made the plebeians and their tribunes important political players, which the earlier laws had failed to do.
lex-manilia: The war against Mithridates, commonly called the Third Mithridatic War, had been conducted by Lucius Licinius Lucullus. By the winter of 68–67 BCE he had driven Mithridates out of Pontus and invaded the Armenian empire of his ally Tigranes the Great. His advance stopped when his discontented troops mutinied under the leadership of Publius Clodius Pulcher; many of these Fimbrian legions had been in the East since the command of Gaius Flavius Fimbria in 86 BCE.

Mithridates and Tigranes took their chance. Mithridates invaded Pontus and Tigranes Cappadocia, and in the summer of 67 BCE Mithridates inflicted a crushing defeat on Roman forces under Lucullus's legate Triarius at the Battle of Zela. Lucullus was superseded by the consul of 67 BCE, Manius Acilius Glabrio, who, seeing the difficulty of the situation, lingered in Bithynia. By the end of that year Mithridates had recovered the whole of his former kingdom.

The law recalled the three commanders then in the East, Lucullus in Pontus, Glabrio in Bithynia and Quintus Marcius Rex in Cilicia, and transferred all their legions and the entire conduct of the eastern war to Pompey. He was already in the East, completing the command against the pirates given him by the lex Gabinia of 67 BCE.

That earlier law had been opposed by almost the whole Senate. The proposal of Manilius, by contrast, had the support of many senators and of several eminent former consuls, among them Publius Servilius Vatia Isauricus, Gaius Scribonius Curio, Gaius Cassius Longinus Varus and Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Clodianus. Cicero was serving as praetor when he delivered his speech for it, which survives. Opposition was largely confined to Quintus Hortensius and Quintus Lutatius Catulus, whose arguments against giving Pompey the command Cicero answers at length.

The law was passed in the Comitia Tributa without the violence that had attended the proposal of Gabinius the year before. Pompey soon moved against Mithridates and Tigranes and had defeated both by the end of 65 BCE, though Mithridates was not killed until 63 BCE. Manilius himself was prosecuted twice after leaving office in December 66 BCE. On the first occasion Cicero defended him against a charge of extortion, and the case was dropped in January 65 BCE amid disturbances and violence. On the second he was condemned on a charge of maiestas and went into exile.
liaoning: Liaoning is named after the Liao River, which runs through the province. It divides into highlands in the west, dominated by the Nulu'erhu Mountains, a flat central basin drained by the Liao and Daliao rivers, and hills in the east, where the Changbai and Qianshan mountains extend into the sea as the Liaodong Peninsula. A narrow coastal strip, the Liaoxi Corridor, joins the Liao basin to the North China Plain and ends at the Shanhai Pass of the Great Wall. The Yalu River marks the border with North Korea. The province has also yielded important fossils, among them Sinosauropteryx, announced in 1996 as the first example of a feathered dinosaur.

Before the 3rd century BCE the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples inhabited the area, and about 300 BCE the state of Yan conquered it and set up two commanderies, Liaodong and Liaoxi. As the Han dynasty fell, the warlord Gongsun Du and his family kept a semi-independent state in Liaodong until Cao Wei defeated it in 238. Xianbei states of the Murong tribe then ruled, and in 436 Goguryeo took the Liaodong Peninsula; the Tang dynasty annexed the region during the Goguryeo–Tang War.

After the An Lushan Rebellion the Bohai expanded into Liaodong, and the region was later conquered by the Khitan Liao dynasty, then held by the Jurchen Jin dynasty. Genghis Khan conquered it in 1206, and it was incorporated into the Yuan dynasty. The Ming took control in 1371 and about 1442 began building the Liaodong Wall, mostly an earth dike with moats, against the Oriyanghan and later the Jianzhou Jurchens, who became known as the Manchu.

The Qing conquest brought heavy loss of population: many residents were killed or fled south of the Great Wall, and Ming forces themselves destroyed many cities. In 1661 the civil governor reported that east of the Liao River only Shenyang, Liaoyang and Haicheng were more than nearly empty. The province was set up as Fengtian in 1907, and key battles of the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905, including Port Arthur and Mukden, were fought here. Zhang Zuolin and his son Zhang Xueliang ruled it in the Warlord Era; the name Liaoning was first adopted on 29 January 1929, and Japan invaded in 1931, when it became part of Manchukuo.

Liaoning is a province of north-eastern China with its capital at Shenyang, and the port of Dalian is among its main cities. The population is mostly Han Chinese, with Manchus, Mongols, Hui, Koreans and Xibe; it has the highest number and share of Manchus in China. The Mukden Palace, where the Qing emperors lived before conquering the rest of China, and three Qing imperial tombs are part of World Heritage Sites, as is the Goguryeo site of Wunu Mountain City.
liberalism: Liberal, liberty and libertine all derive from the Latin liber, meaning free. One of the first recorded uses of liberal, in 1375, described the liberal arts as an education desirable for a free-born man. The political tradition is mostly modern and began in the 17th century, although some of its ideas had precursors in classical antiquity and Imperial China. During the English Civil War the Levellers called for freedom of religion, frequent parliaments and equality under the law.

Thomas Hobbes built the idea of a social contract on a hypothetical state of nature and concluded that only an absolute sovereign could guarantee security. John Locke, generally regarded as the father of modern liberalism, took over the state of nature and the contract but argued that government needs the continuing consent of the governed. When a monarch becomes a tyrant, he held, the people have a right to overthrow him, since the contract protects life, liberty and property as natural rights.

Liberalism rests on individual rights, liberty, consent of the governed, political equality, private property and equality before the law. Different liberals understand these principles differently, and scholars often describe its doctrines as containing separate and often contradictory streams of thought. Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776) held that where prices and competition are left free of regulation, the pursuit of self-interest, directed by an invisible hand, maximises a society's wealth. Jean-Baptiste Say and John Stuart Mill carried economic liberalism further, in 1803 and 1848.

Sismondi's New Principles of Political Economy (1819) was the first comprehensive liberal critique of early capitalism. By the end of the 19th century poverty, unemployment and organised labour challenged classical liberalism, and social liberalism emerged. The word now varies by region. In Europe and Latin America it means a moderate form of classical liberalism, while in North America it refers almost exclusively to social liberalism.

The Glorious Revolution of 1688, which entrenched parliamentary sovereignty, has been called the first modern liberal revolution. The American Revolution of 1776, the Constitution of 1787 and the French Revolution of 1789 used liberal philosophy against royal sovereignty. In the 19th century liberal governments were established in Europe and South America, and liberal ideas influenced reform in the Ottoman Empire and the Middle East, including the Tanzimat and Al-Nahda.

Liberalism has had many critics. The Roman Catholic Church was among its earliest and most outspoken. Edmund Burke attacked the liberal faith in rationality and natural equality, and Karl Marx rejected liberal theory. Before 1920 its main opponents were communism, conservatism and socialism, and it then faced fascism and Marxism–Leninism. Liberal ideas spread further in the 20th century, and social liberalism became a key component in expanding the welfare state.
libreville: Libreville stands on the northern bank of the Gabon Estuary, near the Gulf of Guinea, in the north-western province of Estuaire. The city covers 65 square kilometres, and the Komo River passes through it and empties into the ocean. It has a tropical monsoon climate, with a wet season of about nine months from September to May and a short dry season. Its districts include Glass, the first European settlement in Gabon, and Owendo to the south, where the port and the terminus of the Trans-Gabon Railway lie.

The Mpongwe people lived in the area before colonisation. In 1839 the French admiral Édouard Bouët-Willaumez negotiated a trade and protection treaty with the Mpongwe ruler Antchoué Komé Rapontcombo, known to the French as King Denis. American missionaries from New England established a mission at Baraka, on what is now Libreville, in 1842.

In 1846 the French navy, which was tasked with contributing to the British blockade of Africa, captured the Brazilian slave ship L'Elizia near Loango. Fifty-two of the freed captives were resettled on the site in 1849, and the settlement was called Libreville, French for Freetown. After the French Revolution of 1848 and the establishment of the Second Republic, the former slaves held an election to choose the leaders of the new village, and a former slave named Mountier was elected mayor. From its earliest years the town functioned mainly as a trading post. Libreville was the administrative capital of France's Congo-Gabon colony from 1888 until 1904, when the capital moved to Brazzaville, and it exported timber, rubber and cocoa from concessions in the interior.

At independence in 1960 it was a trading post and minor administrative centre with a population of 32,000. It has since grown rapidly. Offshore petroleum discovered in the 1970s financed an expansion of its administration and construction, and the city hosted the Organisation of African Unity summit in 1977. The Trans-Gabon Railway, opened in stages between 1978 and 1986, links Owendo with Franceville.

Libreville is the capital and largest city of Gabon and the seat of its government. It is the country's main commercial and administrative centre and its leading gateway for imports and exports through the port complex at Owendo. French is spoken there, and is becoming a native language for many residents. Landmarks include the Arboretum de Sibang, the Palais du bord de mer and the National Museum of Arts, Rites and Traditions of Gabon, and Omar Bongo University was founded in 1970.
libya: Libya extends over 1,759,540 km2 and has the longest coastline of any African country on the Mediterranean, at 1,770 kilometres. It comprises three historical regions, Tripolitania, Fezzan and Cyrenaica. The climate is mostly extremely dry and desertlike, with a milder Mediterranean climate in the north, and the oases of Ghadames and Kufra are the most important of those scattered through the country.

About 90% of the people live along the coast, in less than 10% of the area. The name Libya first appears as rbw in an inscription of Ramesses II, and the Great Karnak Inscription records a war in 1208 BCE between King Meryey of the Libu and the pharaoh Merneptah, who defeated him. Italian geographer Federico Minutilli brought the name back into use in 1903.

Neolithic peoples inhabited the coastal plain from about 8000 BCE. The Garamantes, based at Germa, are the earliest known tribe by name, and the Phoenicians were the first to establish trading posts. Greeks colonised the area around Barca in 630 BCE and founded Cyrene, and four more Greek cities followed within 200 years. Persian rule began in 525 BCE, Alexander the Great ended it in 331 BCE, and the east then passed to the Ptolemaic Kingdom. Rome annexed Cyrenaica in 74 BCE, and Tripolitania reached a golden age in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, when Leptis Magna, home of the Severan dynasty, was at its height.

Libya was an early centre of Christianity and the home of Pope Victor I. The Vandals mostly held the area after the fall of the Western Roman Empire until the 7th century, when invasions brought Islam. Ottoman rule began in 1551 and continued until Italy occupied Libya in 1911. Italian Libya existed as a unified colony from 1934 to 1943, and Libya became independent as a kingdom in 1951.

Muammar Gaddafi overthrew King Idris I in a bloodless coup in 1969 and ruled for 42 years until he was overthrown and killed in the 2011 civil war. Arabs account for 92% of the population and Berbers for 5%, and there are about 140 tribes and clans.
liguria: Liguria is bordered by France to the west, Piedmont to the north, and Emilia-Romagna and Tuscany to the east, and rests on the Ligurian Sea. Its narrow strip of land is hemmed in by the sea, the Alps and the Apennines, and the watershed runs at an average height of about 1,000 metres. Its coast is the Italian Riviera, which runs from the French border near Ventimiglia east to Capo Corvo, at the end of the Gulf of La Spezia.

The name Liguria predates Latin and has no settled etymology. It comes from the ancient Ligures, whose territory was much larger than the present region: it took in all of north-west Italy south of the Po and part of south-eastern France. Human presence is very old: traces of huts built by nomadic hunters about 300,000 years ago have been found at Terra Amata, near Nice.

In the First Punic War the Ligurians were divided, some siding with Carthage and others, including the people of Stalia, later Genoa, with Rome. In 180 BCE the Romans deported 47,000 Ligures Apuani. Under Augustus the region became Regio IX Liguria, reaching from the coast to the Po. From the 4th to the 10th century it was held by Byzantines, Lombards under King Rothari about 641 and Franks about 774, and invaded by Saracen and Norman raiders. In the 10th century it was divided into three marches, and the coastal towns became city-states under Genoa's growing rule.

French influence ended in 1528, when Andrea Doria allied with the king of Spain and imposed an aristocratic government that gave the republic relative stability for about 250 years. After a short independence in 1814, the Congress of Vienna in 1815 annexed Liguria to the Kingdom of Sardinia. A Genoese uprising against the House of Savoy in 1821 was put down with great bloodshed. Giuseppe Mazzini, Mameli and Nino Bixio of the Risorgimento were born there, and Giuseppe Garibaldi began his Expedition of the Thousand on 5 May 1860 from a rock at Quarto, a quarter of Genoa.

Liguria is a region of Italy with its capital at Genoa and it is roughly coextensive with the former territory of the Republic of Genoa. It is the third smallest Italian region, yet one of the most densely populated. Agriculture is specialised in flowers, wine and olive oil, and the cliffside vineyards of the Cinque Terre produce white wines.
lille: Lille lies along the Deûle river in the northern part of France, within French Flanders and close to the border with Belgium. It is nicknamed in France the Capital of Flanders, and it belongs to the historical region of Romance Flanders. The commune covers only 35 square kilometres, but together with its suburbs it forms a conurbation of several cities, including Roubaix, Tourcoing and Villeneuve-d'Ascq. It also forms part of a cross-border grouping with the Belgian cities of Mouscron, Kortrijk, Tournai and Menin.

Excavations suggest the area was inhabited as early as 2000 BCE, in the districts now called Fives, Wazemmes and Vieux Lille. Its early inhabitants were Gauls such as the Menapians, the Morins, the Atrebates and the Nervians, followed by Germanic peoples including the Saxons, the Frisians and the Franks. A Battle of Lille was fought in 1054. From the 12th century the fame of the Lille cloth fair grew, and the city has been a merchant city since its origins and a manufacturing city since the 16th century.

As a garrison town, protected by its citadel, Lille was often besieged and belonged successively to the Kingdom of France, the Burgundian State, the Holy Roman Empire and the Spanish Netherlands. In 1792, during the aftermath of the French Revolution, Austrian forces besieged it for eight days; their artillery destroyed many houses and the main church, but the city, led by Mayor François André-Bonte, did not surrender. The Column of the Goddess, erected in 1842, commemorates the resistance.

The Industrial Revolution made Lille a great industrial capital, built mainly on textiles and mechanical industries. German forces occupied it on 13 October 1914 after a ten-day siege and heavy shelling that destroyed 882 apartment and office blocks and 1,500 houses. In July 1921 Albert Calmette and Camille Guérin announced at the Pasteur Institute in Lille the first anti-tuberculosis vaccine, known as BCG. In the Second World War the city was occupied again and was liberated in early September 1944 by a British force largely of tanks.

Lille is the capital of the Hauts-de-France region and the prefecture of the Nord department. Its old centre has 17th-century red brick town houses around the Grand'Place, and the belfry of its city hall is among the belfries inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites in July 2005. Other sights include the citadel, the cathedral and the Palais des Beaux-Arts. Charles de Gaulle was born there. The annual Braderie, held on the first weekend of September, is thought to date from the twelfth century. Lille opened the first automatic light metro line in the world in 1983, and Eurostar trains have served it since 1994.
lima: Lima lies in the valleys of the Chillón, Rímac and Lurín rivers, in the desert zone of Peru's central coast, overlooking the Pacific Ocean. The urban area covers about 800 square kilometres on mostly flat terrain, sloping gently from the shore into valleys and mountain slopes as high as 1,550 metres. The seaport and the international airport are in the neighbouring Constitutional Province of Callao, with which the city forms a contiguous urban area.

Before the Spanish founding in 1535 the three valleys were occupied by pre-Inca settlements grouped under the Lordship of Ichma, and the Maranga and Lima cultures took shape there. The sanctuary of Pachacámac, built between the third and fifteenth centuries by several civilisations, was the main pilgrimage site in Inca times. The Wari Empire conquered these cultures and built the ceremonial centre of Cajamarquilla. As Wari power declined, local cultures such as the Chancay regained autonomy, and in the fifteenth century the territory was absorbed into the Inca Empire.

The name probably comes from Limaq, meaning talker or speaker in the coastal Quechua of the area, the name of an oracle in the Rímac Valley that the Spanish destroyed and replaced with a church. The city was founded in 1535 as the City of Kings, because its foundation was decided on 6 January, the feast of the Epiphany. Francisco Pizarro built the first Government Palace, known as the House of Pizarro, that year.

Lima became the capital and most important city of the Viceroyalty of Peru, and the National University of San Marcos, founded in 1551, is the oldest continuously operating university in the New World. After José de San Martín reached the city in 1821 during the Peruvian War of Independence, it was granted the title of Heroic and Courageous City of the Free. It then became the capital of the Republic of Peru.

Lima is the capital and largest city of Peru and the seat of its three branches of government. The Historic Centre was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988. It keeps colonial buildings such as the Basilica and Convent of San Francisco, the Metropolitan Cathedral and the Palacio de Torre Tagle. About a third of the country's people live in its metropolitan area.
linux: Unix was conceived in 1969 at AT&T's Bell Labs, first released in 1971 and rewritten in the C programming language by Dennis Ritchie in 1973, which made it easier to port. Because a 1956 antitrust case forbade AT&T to enter the computer business, it gave the source code to anyone who asked, and Unix spread through universities and businesses. In 1984, freed of that obligation, Bell Labs began selling it as a proprietary product users were not legally allowed to modify.

In response the GNU Project, started in 1983 by Richard Stallman, aimed to create a complete Unix-compatible system made entirely of free software. By the early 1990s many of its programs were finished, but its kernel, GNU Hurd, was stalled. Minix, released in 1987 for teaching, had a licence that kept it from being free software until April 2000, and the first entirely free Unix for personal computers, 386BSD, appeared only in 1992.

Linus Torvalds created the Linux kernel because GNU lacked a working one, and first released it on 17 September 1991. Like GNU and 386BSD it contained no Unix code, so it avoided legal problems with AT&T. It is distributed under the copyleft GNU General Public License, and anyone may use, modify and distribute the source code, commercially or not, which makes creating a new distribution easier than for macOS or Microsoft Windows.

A distribution packages the kernel with software developed by others, such as GNU and X.Org; Debian, Fedora and Ubuntu are examples. The Free Software Foundation recommends the name GNU/Linux, a usage that is controversial. Distributions became popular in the 1990s and made Unix technologies accessible to home users on personal computers, where before they had been confined to sophisticated workstations.

Originally written for x86 personal computers, the kernel has been ported to more platforms than any other operating system. Linux runs on all of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers, and Android uses a Linux-based kernel. Eric S. Raymond saw the revolutionary aspect of Linux as social: huge numbers of volunteers coordinated through the Internet, and quality was kept by releasing every week and gathering feedback from hundreds of users within days.
lisbon: Lisbon lies at the mouth of the Tagus River and is the westernmost capital of a mainland European country. Its sheltered harbour in the Tagus estuary was an ideal site for an early settlement, a secure place to unload and provision trading ships. The city occupies about 100 square kilometres, and its boundaries coincide with those of the municipality. The Monsanto Forest Park takes up 10% of it. The climate is Mediterranean, with mild, rainy winters and warm to hot, dry summers.

During the Neolithic period pre-Celtic tribes built megaliths, dolmens and menhirs, some of which survive on the edge of the city. Iron Age people occupied the site of the Castelo hill from the 8th to the 6th century BCE and traded with the Phoenicians, and a Phoenician trading post stood on the southern slope of the hill. The settlement traded with inland tribes, supplying metals, salt, salted fish and Lusitanian horses. Julius Caesar made it a municipium called Felicitas Julia, adding that term to the name Olisipo.

After the fall of the Roman Empire it was ruled by Germanic tribes from the 5th century, most notably the Visigoths, and was captured by the Moors in the 8th century. Afonso Henriques conquered it in 1147, and in 1255 it replaced Coimbra as capital of Portugal. The population was about 35,000 in 1300, 70,000 by 1500 and almost 200,000 in 1700.

Lisbon is the seat of the Portuguese government, the Assembly of the Republic and the Supreme Court of Justice. Its architecture includes Romanesque, Gothic, Manueline and Baroque buildings, and its museums include the National Museum of Ancient Art, the National Coach Museum and the Gulbenkian Museum. Yellow trams, introduced in 1901, still run on the hills of the central city.
lithuania: Lithuania lies on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea, bordered by Latvia to the north, Belarus to the east and south, Poland to the south and the Russian semi-exclave of Kaliningrad Oblast to the southwest. It covers 65,300 square kilometres and has around 99 kilometres of sandy coastline, much of it sheltered by the Curonian sand peninsula. The warm-water port of Klaipėda lies at the mouth of the Curonian Lagoon.

The landscape was smoothed by the glaciers of the last ice age and combines moderate lowlands and highlands, with numerous lakes and wetlands. The highest point is Aukštojas Hill at 294 metres. A mixed forest zone covers over 33% of the country, and the Nemunas River carries international shipping.

The first people settled after the Last Glacial Period, in the 10th millennium BCE, as travelling hunters of the Kunda, Neman and Narva cultures. Indo-Europeans arrived in the 3rd to 2nd millennium BCE and mixed with the local population to form the Baltic tribes, who kept trade contacts through the Amber Road. From the 9th to the 11th centuries coastal Balts were raided by Vikings. The remoteness of the area accounts for its separate linguistic, cultural and religious identity, and traditional pagan customs were long preserved.

The first known record of the name Lietuva is a 1009 story of Saint Bruno in the Annals of Quedlinburg. In the 1230s Lithuanian lands were united for the first time by Mindaugas, who formed the Kingdom of Lithuania on 6 July 1253. The Grand Duchy of Lithuania was the largest country in Europe by the 14th century. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was dismantled by neighbouring countries between 1772 and 1795, and Russia annexed most of Lithuanian territory.

Lithuania declared independence in 1918, and on 11 March 1990 it became the first Soviet republic to proclaim the restoration of its independence. It has a semi-presidential system: the president is directly elected for five years, and the Seimas has 141 members elected to four-year terms. The euro replaced the litas on 1 January 2015.

The population is 2.9 million, and 82.6% of residents were ethnic Lithuanians in 2024, with Poles (6.3%) and Russians (5.0%) the largest minorities. Lithuanian is a Baltic language believed to be the linguistically most conservative living Indo-European tongue. The first grammar, Grammatica Litvanica, was published in Latin in 1653 by Danielius Kleinas.
liverpool: Liverpool lies on the eastern side of the Mersey Estuary, near the Irish Sea, about 286 kilometres north-west of London. It is built across a ridge of sandstone hills. The name comes from the Old English lifer, meaning thick or muddy water, and pōl, a pool or creek, and is first recorded around 1190 as Liuerpul. The reference was to a tidal creek, now filled in, into which two streams drained.

Liverpool was established as a borough in Lancashire in 1207. In the Middle Ages it grew from farmland into a small town of farmers, fishermen and tradesmen and a base for King John. A tidal creek called the Pool gave ships a natural harbour. Disease and its subordination to the nearby port of Chester kept its growth from advancing until the late 17th and early 18th centuries. The Old Dock, opened in 1715, was the world's first enclosed wet dock. In the late 17th century the port became heavily involved in the Atlantic slave trade, and it also imported cotton for the Lancashire textile mills and became a major departure point for emigrants to North America.

The 19th century brought global economic importance and a run of firsts: the first inter-city railway, the first non-combustible warehouse system at the Royal Albert Dock, built in 1846 under Jesse Hartley, transatlantic steamships and a pioneering elevated electric railway. Liverpool was granted city status in 1880 and in 1974 moved from Lancashire to the new county of Merseyside. In the 20th century its position as a seaport made it vulnerable in the two world wars, and economic depressions and the containerisation of shipping contributed to decline, which was largely reversed after it was selected as European Capital of Culture for 2008.

Liverpool is a port city and metropolitan borough in Merseyside, England, and the core of the Liverpool City Region, which has over 1.5 million people. It has over 2,500 listed buildings, among them Speke Hall, a Tudor manor house completed in 1598, and English Heritage has described it as England's finest Victorian city. The Royal Albert Dock now houses the Merseyside Maritime Museum, the International Slavery Museum and Tate Liverpool. It is the birthplace of the Beatles, and Liverpool Lime Street is the world's oldest still-operating main line railway station.
livorno: The origins of Livorno are controversial, although the place was inhabited from the Neolithic, as bones, copper and ceramic found in a cave between Ardenza and Montenero show. The Etruscan settlement was called Labro. Livorna is mentioned for the first time in 1017 as a small coastal village and port, with the remains of a Roman tower, under the rule of Lucca. A tower was built by Matilda of Tuscany in 1077, and the Republic of Pisa owned the place from 1103 and built a quadrangular fort, the Quadratura dei Pisani, to defend the port. Porto Pisano was destroyed after the Pisan fleet was crushingly defeated at the Battle of Meloria in 1284.

After the Medici, the ruling dynasty of Florence, arrived, the Fortezza Vecchia was built between 1518 and 1534 and voluntary resettlement of the population was encouraged, though Livorno remained a rather insignificant coastal fortress, with 1,562 residents by 1551. It became the seat of the crusading and corsairing Order of Saint Stephen after 1561, distinctive for its aggressive approach towards the Muslim world, and a major Mediterranean slave trade hub in the early modern period, rivalling Malta's, with a slave population that may have exceeded 25 per cent of its inhabitants. Designed as an ideal town in the Renaissance, it developed considerably from the second half of the 16th century, and its intense commercial activity was largely dominated by foreign traders.

At the end of the 17th century Livorno underwent a period of great urban planning and expansion, with a new fortress, town walls and a system of navigable canals through its neighbourhoods. The port of Pisa had silted up in the 13th century, so Livorno took over as the main port of Tuscany, the seat of consulates and shipping companies. Its population had risen to 32,534 by 1745. Its high status as a multiethnic, multicultural city lasted until the second half of the 19th century, when other cities surpassed it.

Livorno is a port city on the western coast of Tuscany, the capital of the Province of Livorno, with 152,451 inhabitants. Its people speak a variant of Tuscan known as a vernacolo, and the Jewish community once used bagitto, a Judæo-Italian dialect with Spanish and Portuguese words from Jews expelled from the Iberian peninsula in the late 15th century.
livy: Livy was born in Patavium, modern Padua, probably in 59 BCE. His city was then the second wealthiest on the Italian peninsula, and it was known for conservative values in morality and politics. His teenage years fell in the civil wars of the 40s BCE. When the governor Asinius Pollio tried to bring Patavium over to Mark Antony, the wealthy citizens refused money and arms and pledged their allegiance to the Senate. The wars probably kept Livy from a higher education in Rome. Pollio later mocked his Latin for its patavinity, the provincialisms of Patavium.

Livy probably went to Rome in the 30s BCE but never became a senator or held office. Mistakes in his work on military matters suggest that he never served in the army. He was educated in philosophy and rhetoric, and had the means to live independently. He knew the emperor Augustus and encouraged the future emperor Claudius to write history.

His history of Rome, Ab Urbe Condita, told the story of the city from the legends before its traditional founding in 753 BCE through the reign of Augustus. He began it when already past his youth, probably at 33, and worked on it until he left Rome for Padua in old age. Together with Polybius he is one of the main accounts of the Second Punic War. Because he wrote under Augustus, his history stresses the triumphs of Rome and embellishes Roman heroism, in order to support the new form of government. Since he mostly described events hundreds of years old, its historical value has been questioned, although many Romans came to believe his account.

Livy died at Patavium in 17 CE. The ancient evidence for his dates is a chronicle of Eusebius, in Jerome's Latin version, whose manuscripts disagree, so that no standard dates exist for him; one manuscript puts his birth in 57 BCE.

His history was in high demand from its publication. Later writers such as Eutropius, Florus and Orosius drew on it. In the Middle Ages readers used summaries, since copying the whole was costly, and manuscripts were lost. In the Renaissance large sums changed hands for Livian manuscripts, and Petrarch and Pope Nicholas V searched for the missing books. Niccolò Machiavelli presented his Discourses on Livy as a commentary on the history.
ljubljana: Ljubljana lies in the Ljubljana Basin in Central Slovenia, between the Alps and the Karst, along a trade route between the northern Adriatic Sea and the Danube region and north of the country's largest marsh. The city centre sits on the Ljubljanica river at 298 metres, and Ljubljana Castle stands on Castle Hill to the south. The city stretches over an alluvial plain, and earthquakes have repeatedly devastated it, notably in 1511 and 1895. It lies some 250 km east of Venice, 124 km west of Zagreb and 350 km south-west of Vienna. Its symbol is the Ljubljana Dragon, which appears on the tower of the castle, on the coat of arms and on the Dragon Bridge.

Around 2000 BCE people living in pile dwellings settled the Ljubljana Marsh. Its prehistoric pile dwellings and the oldest wooden wheel in the world are among the notable finds, and the remains have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since June 2011. The area later served as a transit point for the Illyrians, the Iapodes and, from the 3rd century BCE, a Celtic tribe, the Taurisci. Around 50 BCE the Romans built a military encampment that became a permanent settlement called Iulia Aemona, held by the Legio XV Apollinaris. It housed 5,000 to 6,000 inhabitants. The Huns destroyed it in 452 on Attila's orders, and later the Ostrogoths and Lombards did the same.

The city was first mentioned in the first half of the 12th century, and the German name Laibach is documented from 1144. It was the historical capital of Carniola, a Slovene-inhabited part of the Habsburg monarchy, and was under Habsburg rule from the Middle Ages until 1918. It was the capital of the Illyrian Provinces from 1809 to 1814. After the Second World War it became the capital of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia within Yugoslavia, and in 1991 the capital of independent Slovenia. In the 19th century tension between German and Slovene residents shaped even the city's sport, and the Ljubljana Sokol gymnastic club, founded in 1863 and succeeded in 1868, served Slovene cultural and political aims.

Ljubljana is the capital and largest city of Slovenia, with about 300,000 inhabitants, and its cultural, educational, economic and political centre. After the earthquake of 1511 it was rebuilt in the Baroque style on Italian, especially Venetian, models, and after that of 1895 in the Vienna Secession style. The architect Jože Plečnik shaped large parts of the inter-war city, and Tivoli City Park, laid out in 1813 during the French administration, was renovated by him between 1921 and 1939.
lodz: Łódź first appears in a written record of 1332, issued by Władysław the Hunchback, Duke of Łęczyca, which transferred the village of Łodzia to the Bishopric of Włocławek. King Władysław II Jagiełło granted it town rights in 1423. For centuries it was a small remote settlement among woodlands and marshes, privately held by the Kuyavian bishops, and its economy rested on agriculture until the 19th century. In 1793 it passed to Prussia, and in 1815 it joined Congress Poland.

In 1820 the Congress Kingdom designated Łódź for centrally planned industrial development. Rajmund Rembieliński headed a commission that created a new city centre around an octagonal square and then cotton mill colonies along a main street, Piotrkowska. Growth was rapid from 1850, with many Jewish and German migrants. The population rose from 13,000 in 1840 to over 500,000 in 1913. Władysław Reymont's novel The Promised Land documents the city's social inequalities.

Łódź became the capital of its voivodeship in 1919. German forces took the city in September 1939, and it was incorporated into Reichsgau Wartheland and renamed Litzmannstadt in April 1940. Its large Jewish minority was forced into the walled Litzmannstadt Ghetto and from there sent to concentration and extermination camps. Soviet forces liberated the city on 19 January 1945, and it temporarily took over the functions of the capital before Warsaw was rebuilt. The National Film School opened in 1948. After 1989 the textile industry collapsed and the city declined.

Łódź is a city in central Poland, 120 kilometres south-west of Warsaw and the capital of Łódź Voivodeship. Piotrkowska Street, a little over five kilometres long, is its main commercial street. Its industrial heritage and Polish Art Nouveau architecture attract visitors, and the National Film School trained directors such as Andrzej Wajda and Roman Polański. Muzeum Sztuki, founded in 1931, was the first museum in Europe dedicated to modern art. The city is now a hub for business services, and in 2017 it joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network as a City of Film.
logarithm: The history of logarithms in seventeenth-century Europe saw the discovery of a new function that took analysis beyond the reach of algebraic methods. Before Napier's book of 1614 there were techniques of similar aim, such as prosthaphaeresis, which relies on trigonometric identities, and tables of progressions, which Jost Bürgi developed extensively around 1600. Napier coined the Middle Latin term logarithmus, literally 'ratio-number', from the Greek logos, proportion or ratio, and arithmos, number. The modern view comes from Leonhard Euler, who in the 18th century connected logarithms to the exponential function and introduced the letter e as the base of natural logarithms.

The logarithm of a number to a given base is the exponent the base must be raised to in order to give the number, so that the logarithm of 1000 to base 10 is 3. It is the inverse of exponentiation, as subtraction is of addition. The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms of the factors, and that of a quotient the difference. Three bases are particularly common: 10, the number e, about 2.718, and 2. Base 10 suits calculation by hand, base e is widespread in mathematics because of its simple derivative, and base 2 is used in computer science and information theory.

Henry Briggs compiled the first table in 1617, with the common logarithms of all integers from 1 to 1000 to 14 digits. Because numbers differing by a factor of 10 have logarithms differing by whole numbers, a table needed only the fractional part, the mantissa; the whole part, the characteristic, came from counting digits. Pierre-Simon Laplace called logarithms an admirable artifice that doubled the life of the astronomer by reducing the labour of many months to a few days. Gunter's rule, a logarithmic scale, was invented soon after Napier's work, and William Oughtred made it into the slide rule by setting two such scales to move against each other. Logarithms also underlie the decibel, pH, and the measure of information in bits.
lombardy: Lombardy lies in northern Italy between the Alps and the tributaries of the river Po. It is bordered by the Swiss cantons of Ticino and Grisons to the north, by Trentino-Alto Adige and Veneto to the east, Emilia-Romagna to the south and Piedmont to the west. About 47 per cent of its territory is plain, 41 per cent mountains and 12 per cent hills. The Po forms its southern border for about 210 kilometres,. The name comes from the Lombards, a Germanic people whose name derives from Late Latin Longobardus, perhaps meaning long beard.

The area has been settled since at least the second millennium BCE, and the rock drawings of the Camuni in Valcamonica are well preserved. In the centuries after the fall of the Western Empire it suffered destruction from a series of invasions. After 540 Pavia became the permanent capital of the Ostrogothic Kingdom. The last and most effective invasion was that of the Lombards, who migrated from the Carpathian basin in 568 in fear of the Avars. Their long-lasting reign, with its capital at Pavia, gave the region its name, and Pavia remained the capital of the kingdom of Italy until 1024.

From the late 11th century Lombardy broke into many small autonomous city-states, the medieval communes. In the 15th century the Duchy of Milan was one of the wealthiest states of the Renaissance, and Milan and Mantua were centres of Renaissance culture, with Leonardo da Vinci and Andrea Mantegna. Lombard merchants and bankers traded as far as northern Europe, and the word Lombard came to mean a banker, as in Lombard Street in London. After the Battle of Pavia the Duchy of Milan became a possession of the Habsburgs of Spain, while the east, including Bergamo and Brescia, was controlled by the Republic of Venice.

Austrian rule was restored in 1815 as the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia. The region was an important centre of the Risorgimento, with the Five Days of Milan in March 1848 and the Ten Days of Brescia in 1849. Lombardy was annexed to the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia after the Second Italian War of Independence in 1859, in which it was the main theatre of battle, with fighting at Magenta and Solferino.
Lombardy is the most populous region of Italy, with about 10 million inhabitants, and its capital and largest city is Milan. Eleven of Italy's 58 UNESCO World Heritage Sites are in Lombardy.
lome: Lomé lies on the Gulf of Guinea at the south-western corner of Togo, with its western edge along the border with Ghana, a few hundred metres from the city centre. Its name comes from Alomé, which in the Ewe language means "in the alo trees", a reference to the forest that stood there. Despite its latitude near the equator it has a tropical savanna climate, because it lies in the Dahomey Gap, with annual rainfall of 800 to 900 millimetres.

The city was founded by the Ewes and grew in the 19th century through German, British and African traders. British customs duties on alcohol and tobacco weighed heavily in the neighbouring Gold Coast, and Ewe traders from the Aflao and Keta area chose the nearby coast at Lomé to unload goods out of reach of customs officers. Growth began around 1880, and Hausa caravans from the cola routes joined European firms there. Togoland was created within the German colonial empire on 5 July 1884 by the Treaty of Togoville, signed by Gustav Nachtigal and King Mlapa III.

A road to Kpalimé was begun in 1892. A port opened in 1904 and made Lomé the only maritime contact point of Togo, ruining its rival Aného, and railways reached Aného in 1905, Kpalimé in 1907 and Atakpamé in 1909.

The population was 8,000 in 1914. German discriminatory patents and licences gradually pushed African traders out of import and export. In 1916 German companies were evicted and replaced by British and French firms. The French authorities created a council of notables in 1922, elective from 1925. In January 1923 a Lomé Women's Revolt forced the release of two arrested Duawo leaders, and a tax increase provoked riots in January 1933. The population grew from 30,000 in 1950 to 80,000 in 1960, the year of independence, and 200,000 in 1970.

Lomé is the capital and largest city of Togo, with an urban population of 837,437 and 2,188,376 residents in its metropolitan area at the 2022 census. Its port, with a free zone opened in 1968, handles much of the transit trade of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso. The Lomé Convention between the European Union and African, Caribbean and Pacific countries was first signed there on 28 February 1975, and the Lomé Peace Accord for Sierra Leone on 7 July 1999. The University of Lomé was founded in 1970. Colonial buildings include the Sacred Heart Cathedral in German neo-Gothic style, and the Akodesséwa district holds a fetish market.
lon-nol: Lon Nol was born in Prey Veng Province on 13 November 1913 to a family of mixed Khmer and Chinese descent. He was educated at the Lycée Chasseloup-Laubat in Saigon and at the Cambodian Royal Military Academy. He entered the French colonial civil service in 1937 as a magistrate and by 1946 was governor of Kratie Province. He joined the army in 1952 and fought the Viet Minh. After independence his nationalist Khmer Renovation party became part of the core of the Sangkum, the movement set up by Norodom Sihanouk for the elections of 1955.

He was appointed army chief of staff in 1955, commander-in-chief in 1960 and deputy prime minister in 1963. He became prime minister after the elections of 1966, and the following year troops savagely repressed the Samlaut Uprising in Battambang Province. Injured in a car crash in 1967, he withdrew for a time, then returned as prime minister in 1969 with Prince Sisowath Sirik Matak as his deputy.

On 12 March 1970 the two men closed the port of Sihanoukville to the North Vietnamese and demanded that all North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces leave Cambodia within 72 hours. Lon Nol at first refused to see Sihanouk deposed; on the night of 17 March Sirik Matak, with three army officers, compelled him at gunpoint to sign the necessary documents. Pro-Sihanouk demonstrations on 28 and 29 March were suppressed with several hundred deaths. The republic was declared on 9 October 1970. Sihanouk later claimed that the CIA had planned the coup, but there is no concrete evidence of its involvement.

The regime carried out mass killings of Vietnamese Cambodians. After a stroke in February 1971 Lon Nol's rule grew erratic and authoritarian: he made himself Marshal in April and suspended the National Assembly in October. By 1975 his government held little more than Phnom Penh and the temple of Preah Vihear.

He resigned on 1 April 1975, his name being first on a list of people the Khmer Rouge had vowed to execute, and went to Indonesia and then to Hawaii. In 1979 he settled in Fullerton, California, where he died of a heart condition on 17 November 1985. His brother Lon Non, a minister of the republic, was executed by the Khmer Rouge after the fall of Phnom Penh. Lon Nol called his ideology, a blend of nationalism and mysticism, Neo-Khmerism, and hoped to unite the Khmers of Cambodia with those of the Mekong Delta and Thailand.
london: London stands on the River Thames in southeast England, at the head of a 50-mile (80 km) tidal estuary down to the North Sea. Its ancient core, the City of London, kept its medieval boundaries, while the City of Westminster to the west has been the site of the national government and parliament for centuries. Until 1889 the name London applied officially only to the City of London; since then it has also denoted the County of London and Greater London.

Since the 19th century the name has referred to the metropolis around the City, historically split among the counties of Middlesex, Essex, Surrey, Kent and Hertfordshire. Since 1965 it has largely comprised Greater London, governed by 33 local authorities and the Greater London Authority.

The first major settlement was founded by the Romans around 47 CE, about four years after their invasion of 43 CE. It lasted until about 61 CE, when the Iceni, led by Queen Boudica, stormed it and burnt it to the ground. The rebuilt Londinium prospered and superseded Colchester as the principal city of the Roman province of Britannia in 100. At its height in the 2nd century, Roman London had a population of about 60,000.

After Roman rule collapsed in the early 5th century the walled city was effectively abandoned. From about 500 an Anglo-Saxon settlement known as Lundenwic developed slightly west of the old Roman city, and by about 680 it had become a major port again. Repeated Viking assaults from the 820s brought decline. London grew rapidly in the 19th century and became the world's largest city at the time. It took over as a major financial centre shortly after 1795, when the Dutch Republic collapsed before the Napoleonic armies and many Amsterdam bankers moved there.

Greater London had a population of just over 9.8 million in 2025, and its wider metropolitan area about 15.4 million. In the 2021 census 40.6% of Londoners were foreign-born, and more than 300 languages are spoken in the city. It is governed by two tiers: the Greater London Authority, led by the mayor of London, and 32 borough councils with the City of London Corporation.

London has more than 50 universities and colleges. The London Underground is the world's oldest rapid transit system, and the Royal Observatory at Greenwich defines the Prime Meridian. In 2012 London became the first city to host the Summer Olympics three times, after 1908 and 1948.
lope-de-vega: Lope de Vega was born in Madrid in November 1562, the son of Félix de Vega, an embroiderer, and Francisca Fernández Flores. His friend and biographer Pérez de Montalbán claimed that he was reading Spanish and Latin at the age of five, and Lope himself said that he wrote his first play at twelve, though these statements are probably exaggerations. He studied under the poet Vicente Espinel, at the Jesuit Colegio Imperial and at the University of Alcalá, but did not take a degree.

In 1583 he served in the Spanish Navy at the Battle of Ponta Delgada in the Azores. Attacks on a former lover, Elena Osorio, and her family led to a libel conviction and banishment from the court. He married Isabel de Alderete y Urbina on 10 May 1588 and sailed with the Armada weeks later on the ship San Juan, one of those that returned to Spain.

After the Armada Lope lived in Valencia, where he refined his technique of weaving two plots into one play. He then served noble households in Toledo and Alba de Tormes, where he wrote the pastoral novel La Arcadia. Isabel died in 1594. Back in Madrid from 1595, he married Juana de Guardo in 1598 and from 1607 was secretary to the Duke of Sessa. After the deaths of his son Carlos Félix and of Juana he was ordained a priest on 24 May 1614, and in 1627 he was admitted to the Order of Malta. He died of scarlet fever in Madrid on 27 August 1635.

Lope established the three-act comedia as the standard form of Spanish drama. In his Arte nuevo de hacer comedias (1609) he defended breaking the neoclassical unities, arguing that the public who paid for plays cared nothing for them. He drew on Spanish history, the Bible, mythology and daily life, and his best-known plays are of the cloak-and-dagger type, among them El perro del hortelano and El castigo sin venganza. Many were written quickly and to order.

By his own records he had composed 230 comedias by 1604, 800 by 1618 and 1,500 by 1632. Of 637 plays known by title, about 450 survive. His poetry includes the Rimas (1604), the religious Rimas sacras (1614) and Rimas humanas y divinas del licenciado Tomé de Burguillos (1634), which is considered his poetic masterpiece.
lord-byron: George Gordon Byron was born on 22 January 1788 in Holles Street, London. He was the only child of Captain John Byron and his second wife, Catherine Gordon, heiress of the Gight estate in Aberdeenshire. Born with a deformity of his right foot, he suffered from a limp that caused him lifelong misery, and he called himself le diable boîteux, the limping devil.

He attended Aberdeen Grammar School from 1795 and Harrow School from 1801 to 1805, an undistinguished student who nevertheless played in the first Eton v Harrow cricket match at Lord's in 1805. He later studied at Trinity College, Cambridge. His first volume of poems, Fugitive Pieces, written when he was 17, was recalled and burned on a friend's advice because of its amorous verses.

Byron took his seat in the House of Lords on 13 March 1809 and left London for the Continent that June. In his first speech to the Lords, on 27 February 1812, he opposed a death penalty for the Luddite frame breakers of Nottinghamshire. His affair with Lady Caroline Lamb, who called him mad, bad and dangerous to know, shocked the British public.

Under pressure from creditors after the break-up of his domestic life, he left England in 1816 and never returned. That summer he settled at the Villa Diodati by Lake Geneva with his physician John William Polidori, and befriended Percy Bysshe Shelley and Mary Godwin. Kept indoors by rain, the group devised tales: Mary Shelley began what became Frankenstein, and Polidori wrote The Vampyre, inspired by a fragment of Byron's. He then lived for seven years in Italy.

His major works include Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Manfred and Hebrew Melodies. Don Juan, a poem of 17 cantos, ranks among the most important long poems published in England since Paradise Lost. He was also a bitter opponent of Lord Elgin's removal of the Parthenon marbles and denounced it in The Curse of Minerva.

In Greece Byron joined the war of independence against the Ottoman Empire and took part of the rebel army under his command despite his lack of military experience. He fell ill on 15 February 1824, bloodletting weakened him, and after catching a cold in April he died of a fever at Missolonghi on 19 April. A month later his Memoirs were burned in the offices of his publisher, John Murray. Greeks revere him as a folk hero.
lorraine: Lorraine is the only French region to border three other countries: Belgium, Luxembourg and Germany. Most of it lies in the Paris Basin, a plateau cut by river valleys, with the sharper relief of the Vosges in the east. The Moselle, the Meurthe and the Meuse run through it. Its position at the crossroads of four nations made it a strategic asset, and its rulers intermarried with royal families across Europe. Two languages are traditionally native to the region, the Romance language Lorrain in the south-east and Lorraine Franconian in the north and west.

The Treaty of Prüm of 855 divided Middle Francia in three, and the northern third, Lotharingia, went to Lothair II. Its rulers were called dukes from 903 and could side nominally with the eastern or western Carolingian kingdoms. In 959 it was split into Upper and Lower Lorraine; the lower duchy was defunct by the end of the 12th century. Lorraine and Bar were joined in a personal union in 1480, made permanent in 1506. France annexed Metz, Verdun and Toul in 1552, which the Empire recognised only in 1648, and annexed Lorraine and Bar themselves in 1766.

In 1871 Germany took the area of the present department of Moselle as part of Alsace-Lorraine and favoured German in administration and schooling. The Treaty of Versailles returned it to France. Nazi Germany annexed it again during the Second World War, and the Cross of Lorraine became the symbol of the Free French Forces under Charles de Gaulle.

Lorraine was an administrative region of France from 1982 until January 2016, made up of Meurthe-et-Moselle, Meuse, Moselle and Vosges, and is now part of the region Grand Est. Nancy, the seat of the duchy for centuries, is the largest metropolitan area. The last iron ore mine closed in 1997 and the last coal mines of the Saar-Lorraine basin in 2004. The region gave its name to quiche Lorraine.
los-angeles: Most of the city lies in the Los Angeles Basin beside the Pacific Ocean, extending partly through the Santa Monica Mountains and north into the San Fernando Valley. The eastern end of the Santa Monica Mountains runs from Downtown to the Pacific and separates the basin from the valley. The city covers about 1,302 square kilometres in all, including 88 square kilometres of water, and extends 71 km from north to south and 47 km from east to west. Its highest point is Mount Lukens, at 1,547 metres, in the foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains.

The Los Angeles Basin and the San Fernando Valley were dominated by the Tongva, later also called the Gabrieleño. The historic centre of Tongva power was the settlement of Yaanga, a name translated as 'place of the poison oak', which became the site where the Spanish founded the pueblo. Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo claimed the area for Spain in 1542, and Gaspar de Portolà and the Franciscan missionary Juan Crespí reached the present site on 2 August 1769.

On 4 September 1781, 44 settlers known as Los Pobladores founded El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles, 'The Town of Our Lady the Queen of the Angels'. The town became part of the First Mexican Empire in 1821. At the end of the Mexican–American War in 1848, Los Angeles and the rest of California passed to the United States under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, and the city was incorporated on 4 April 1850, five months before California became a state. Oil discovered in the 1890s brought rapid growth, and the Los Angeles Aqueduct, completed in 1913, brought water from Eastern California.

Los Angeles is the most populous city in California and the commercial, financial and cultural centre of Southern California, with 3,898,747 residents counted in the 2020 census. It is the county seat of Los Angeles County and a charter city governed by a mayor and a city council. Well over 200 languages are spoken there. The city hosted the Summer Olympics in 1932 and 1984, and is one of the oldest and largest hubs of film and television production.
louis-armstrong: Armstrong was born and raised in New Orleans, to Mary Estelle Albert, known as Mayann, and William Armstrong, who abandoned the family soon after. He was raised by his grandmother until the age of five, grew up in poverty in a rough neighbourhood known as the Battlefield, and at six began attending the Fisk School for Boys, which accepted black children in the segregated school system. In the late 1910s he played in brass bands and on riverboats, travelling up and down the Mississippi with the band of Fate Marable, who insisted that his musicians learn to read music. In 1918 his mentor Joe King Oliver left Kid Ory's band for the north, and Armstrong replaced him.

In 1922 Armstrong moved to Chicago at Oliver's invitation and played second cornet in Oliver's Creole Jazz Band. In 1924 he went to New York to play with the Fletcher Henderson Orchestra, the top African-American band of the time, switching to the trumpet. He returned to Chicago in 1925, formed Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five, and recorded Potato Head Blues and Muggles. In 1929 his version of Ain't Misbehavin', sung in the revue Hot Chocolates, became his biggest-selling record.

In 1943 he settled permanently in Queens, New York, with his fourth wife, Lucille. By the 1950s he was an international icon, though young jazz musicians such as Charlie Parker and Miles Davis found his half-entertainer style outmoded. He made three records with Ella Fitzgerald, and his 1964 recording of Hello, Dolly! won a Grammy Award.

Armstrong was a foundational influence in jazz, shifting its focus from collective improvisation to solo performance, and he was also an influential singer, skilled at scat. His Melancholy Blues is on the Voyager Golden Record, sent into space. He rarely discussed racial issues in public, to the dismay of some black Americans. In 1957, shortly after the school desegregation conflict in Little Rock, Arkansas, he denounced Governor Orval Faubus and President Dwight D. Eisenhower in an interview and said he would cancel a State Department tour of the Soviet Union. The FBI kept a file on him, and the remarks drew praise from Jackie Robinson and Lena Horne and a ban of his records by a Mississippi radio station.
louis-pasteur: Louis Pasteur was born on 27 December 1822 in Dole, Jura, France, to a Catholic family; his father, Jean-Joseph Pasteur, was a poor tanner. The family moved to Marnoz in 1826 and to Arbois in 1827. He was dyslexic and dysgraphic, and as a boy was an average student whose interests were fishing and sketching.

He studied at the Collège d'Arbois and, from 1839, the Collège Royal at Besançon, earning a Bachelor of Science in Mathematics at Dijon in 1842, but with a mediocre grade in chemistry. He passed the entrance test for the École Normale Supérieure with a high ranking in 1843 and in 1847 submitted two theses, one in chemistry and one in physics, while working as a graduate laboratory assistant for the chemist Antoine Jérôme Balard.

Pasteur became professor of chemistry at the University of Strasbourg in 1848. In 1854 he was named dean of the new faculty of sciences at the University of Lille, where he began his studies on fermentation. In 1857 he moved to Paris as director of scientific studies at the École Normale Supérieure, which he directed from 1858 to 1867, introducing reforms that raised its standards. His rigid decrees led to two student revolts, and when he threatened to expel any student caught smoking, 73 of the 80 students resigned.

He established the Pasteur Institute in 1887 and directed it for the rest of his life. He married Marie Laurent in 1849, and three of their five children died young. Pasteur died on 28 September 1895, and his body was interred in a vault beneath the institute.

In 1848 Pasteur resolved a problem about tartaric acid. The compound derived from living things rotated polarised light, while the chemically synthesised one did not. He found that crystals of tartrates in racemic mixtures were half right-handed and half left-handed, and he concluded that an asymmetric internal arrangement of the molecules was responsible. This was the first demonstration of molecular chirality and the first explanation of isomerism.

In 1856 a local wine manufacturer asked his advice, and Pasteur began research on fermentation. His experiments with sterilised flasks disproved spontaneous generation and won him the Alhumbert Prize in 1862. He supported the germ theory of disease, and he is best known for treating milk and wine to stop bacterial contamination, a process named pasteurization. In 1878 he told his family never to reveal his notebooks, and the historian Gerald Geison argued in 1995 that they showed misleading accounts of his discoveries, a view Max Perutz contested.
louis-xiv: Louis XIV was born on 5 September 1638 at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye to Louis XIII and Anne of Austria, who had been married for 23 years. He was named Louis Dieudonné, the God-given, and contemporaries regarded his birth as a miracle. When Louis XIII died in 1643, a regency council headed by Anne ruled for his four-year-old son, and Anne picked Cardinal Mazarin as chief minister. As the Thirty Years' War ended, a civil war known as the Fronde broke out in France. Louis was declared of age on 7 September 1651, and when Mazarin died in March 1661 he took the government into his own hands and declared that he would rule without a chief minister.

Believing in the divine right of kings, Louis compelled many nobles to live at his palace of Versailles, which pacified an aristocracy many of whom had joined the Fronde. His Great Ordinance of Civil Procedure of 1667, the Code Louis, imposed uniform civil procedure on a kingdom that had been a patchwork of legal systems, and later became the basis for the Napoleonic Code. In 1682 La Salle followed the Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico and claimed its basin for Louis as Louisiane.

Warfare defined his foreign policy. The War of Devolution began in 1667 after the death of Philip IV of Spain, since Maria Theresa's Spanish dowry was never paid. The Nine Years' War, from 1688 to 1697, ended with the Peace of Ryswick, which left Louis permanent sovereignty over Alsace, including Strasbourg. In 1700 Charles II of Spain left his empire to Louis's grandson Philip, Duke of Anjou, and the War of the Spanish Succession followed, ending in the Peace of Utrecht in 1713. Louis also revoked the Edict of Nantes, which had given Huguenots political and religious freedom, and the persecution that followed virtually destroyed the French Protestant community.

Louis outlived most of his legitimate family: his son the Dauphin died of smallpox in 1711, his grandson the Duke of Burgundy of measles a year later, and Burgundy's elder son a few weeks after that. His heir on his deathbed was a five-year-old great-grandson. He died on 1 September 1715, leaving a powerful but war-weary kingdom in major debt. According to Philippe de Courcillon's journal he advised his heir not to follow his example of undertaking war too lightly. He patronised Molière, Racine, Lully and Le Brun, and the saying "I am the state" attributed to him is apocryphal.
louis-xvi: Louis-Auguste was born at the Palace of Versailles on 23 August 1754 and given the title Duke of Berry. He was the second surviving son of Louis, the Dauphin, and Marie-Josèphe of Saxony, and became Dauphin himself when his father died in 1765. On 19 April 1770, at fifteen, he married the fourteen-year-old Archduchess Maria Antonia of Austria, the Marie Antoinette of history, a daughter of Empress Maria Theresa.

He came to the throne on 10 May 1774, aged nineteen, when the government was deeply in debt and resentment of despotic monarchy was growing. His grandfather Louis XV had been widely hated by the time of his death, and the monarchy had spent heavily on unsuccessful wars. The young king felt woefully unqualified to resolve the situation.

The first part of his reign was marked by attempts at reform in line with Enlightenment ideas, among them greater tolerance of non-Catholics and the abolition of the death penalty for deserters. The nobility reacted with hostility, and the parlements blocked the financial reforms of Turgot and Malesherbes, who were removed in 1776. Jacques Necker then borrowed abroad instead of raising taxes, and his Compte-rendu of 1781 led the public to think that the kingdom ran a modest surplus.

Louis supported the American colonists from 1776, first by sending supplies in secret, and in 1778 by a formal Treaty of Alliance and war with Britain. The ensuing debt and financial crisis contributed to the unpopularity of the ancien régime. The Estates General met in 1789, and the storming of the Bastille forced him to recognise the legislative authority of the National Assembly. On 5 October 1789 a mob from Paris marched on Versailles, and the royal family was taken to the Tuileries Palace in Paris.

On 21 June 1791 Louis tried to flee secretly with his family to the fortress town of Montmédy, where he hoped to join the émigrés and be protected by Austria. The attempt failed at Varennes and seemed to confirm that he hoped for foreign intervention, which undermined his legitimacy. Louis was arrested during the Insurrection of 10 August 1792. The monarchy was abolished on 21 September 1792, and he became Citizen Louis Capet.

The National Convention tried him, found him guilty of high treason and had him guillotined on 21 January 1793. His death ended more than a thousand years of continuous French monarchy. Both his sons died in childhood, and his only child to reach adulthood, Marie Thérèse, was exchanged for French prisoners of war and died childless in 1851.
louvre: The Louvre stands on the Right Bank of the Seine in the 1st arrondissement of Paris, next to the Tuileries Gardens. The museum occupies the Louvre Palace, which King Philip II began in the late 12th century to protect the city from attack from the west, since the Kingdom of England then still held Normandy. Remnants of the medieval fortress are visible in the basement.

As the city grew, the fortress lost its defensive function, and in 1546 Francis I converted it into the main residence of the French kings. In 1682 Louis XIV chose Versailles for his household, leaving the Louvre mainly as a place to display the royal collection, which from 1692 included ancient Greek and Roman sculptures. In 1699 the first of a series of salons of the Académie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture was held there.

In May 1791 the National Constituent Assembly declared that the Louvre would be a place for bringing together monuments of all the sciences and arts. After Louis XVI was imprisoned on 10 August 1792 the royal collection became national property, and the museum opened on 10 August 1793 with 537 paintings, mostly royal and confiscated church property. In 1802 Napoleon appointed Vivant Denon its first director, and in 1803 it was renamed Musée Napoléon. The collection grew with the spoils of the Napoleonic wars, though many works were returned to their owners after 1815.

Napoleon III transformed the building and the museum, and between 1852 and 1870 it added 20,000 artefacts. On 23 May 1871 Communards set fire to the adjoining Tuileries Palace, and the fire spread to the museum's north-west wing, but firemen and museum staff saved it. In 1981 President François Mitterrand proposed the Grand Louvre plan, which moved the Finance Ministry out of the North Wing so that almost the whole building could serve the museum. I. M. Pei's design of 1984 added an underground entrance reached through a glass pyramid in the Cour Napoléon.

The Louvre is a national art museum owned by the French government. Its collection is divided into eight departments: Egyptian Antiquities; Near Eastern Antiquities; Greek, Etruscan and Roman Antiquities; Islamic Art; Sculpture; Decorative Arts; Paintings; and Prints and Drawings. Among its best-known works are the Mona Lisa, the Venus de Milo and the Winged Victory of Samothrace. The Near Eastern department dates from 1881 and grew from Paul-Émile Botta's 1843 expedition to Khorsabad, where he found the palace of Sargon II.
lower-austria: Lower Austria occupies the north-eastern corner of Austria and has a land area of 19,186 square kilometres. It borders the Czech Republic and Slovakia along a frontier of 414 kilometres, and the Austrian states of Upper Austria, Styria and Burgenland, and it surrounds Vienna.
