Almost all of it is drained by the Danube; the only river that flows to the North Sea, by way of the Vltava and the Elbe, is the Lainsitz in the north of the Waldviertel.

The land is divided into four quarters. The Mostviertel lies above the Vienna Woods and rises to the foothills of the Limestone Alps, the Industrieviertel lies below them, the Weinviertel is a hilly region below the Manhartsberg, and the Waldviertel above it is mostly a granite plateau. The state is rich in karst caves, with 4,082 recorded.

Human settlement here is old. At Schletz, in the area of the Linear Pottery culture, more than 200 Neolithic people were killed in a massacre some 7,000 years ago. Klosterneuburg Abbey is one of the oldest abbeys in Austria. The names Lower Austria and Upper Austria derive from the earlier Austria below the Enns and Austria above the Enns, after the river Enns, and in the middle of the 13th century the land became known as the Principality below the Enns.

The Battle on the Marchfeld, fought on 26 August 1278, marked the beginning of the ascendancy of the House of Habsburg in Austria and Central Europe. During the Ottoman wars in Europe the region was repeatedly raided by Tatars and Ottoman Akinji, irregular mounted troops, and many people were taken into slavery. In 1809 it was the site of the Battles of Aspern and Wagram, fought between French troops under Napoleon and an Austrian army led by Archduke Charles. Before the Second World War Lower Austria had the largest number of Jews in the country.

Lower Austria is the largest of the nine states of Austria and has a population of about 1.7 million. Vienna became a separate state in 1921, and Sankt Pölten has been the capital since 1986. The state has 20 districts, four independent towns and 573 municipalities. The Wachau valley between Melk and Krems is known for its landscape, culture and wine.
lower-saxony: Lower Saxony covers 47,614 km2 and is the second-largest German state by land area. It is the only state that has both a sea coast and mountains: the North Sea and the East Frisian Islands lie in the north-west, the North German Plain fills the northern half, and the Weser Uplands and the Harz Mountains rise to the south. The state of Bremen forms two enclaves inside it, the city of Bremen and its seaport Bremerhaven.

In the north-east lies the Lüneburg Heath, the largest heathland area of Germany. In the Middle Ages the town of Lüneburg was wealthy from salt-mining and the salt trade. West of Hamburg, the Altes Land on the Elbe is the state's largest fruit-farming area, with apples as its chief produce.

The name Saxony derives from the Saxons, a Germanic confederation of tribes. Before the late medieval period there was a single Duchy of Saxony. After the stem duchy was dissolved in the late 13th century, the term Lower Saxony came into use for the parts of it ruled by the House of Welf, to distinguish them from the Electorate of Saxony on one side and the Duchy of Westphalia on the other.

The modern state was created from parts of the British occupation zone after the Second World War. On 1 November 1946 the State of Hanover, a former kingdom that had been a province of Prussia since 1866, was merged with the three smaller free states of Brunswick, Oldenburg and Schaumburg-Lippe. Because most of the territory had belonged to the Kingdom of Hanover, the new state took over its coat of arms, a white Saxon horse on a red ground.

The first Landtag, appointed by the British administration, met on 9 December 1946 and elected the Social Democrat Hinrich Wilhelm Kopf as minister-president. He led a five-party coalition whose task was to improve food supplies and rebuild the cities and towns destroyed by Allied air raids.

Lower Saxony has about 8 million inhabitants, and its capital and largest city is Hanover. It is divided into 37 districts and several urban districts, and its constitution describes it as a free, republican, democratic, social and environmentally sustainable state within the Federal Republic of Germany. Agriculture, especially livestock farming, has long been important to its economy. The state has four World Heritage Sites, and Northern Low Saxon and Saterland Frisian are still spoken in rural areas.
lu-xun: Lu Xun was born Zhou Zhangshou on 25 September 1881 in Shaoxing, Zhejiang, into a declining family of landlords and scholar-officials. In 1893 his father was found trying to bribe an examination official and lost his position; his grandfather was sentenced to beheading for the offence, a sentence commuted to imprisonment, and he was released in 1901 only after regular, expensive bribes. His father died in 1896 at the age of 35. Lu Xun's early education rested on the Confucian classics, which he later found neither useful nor interesting; he preferred folk stories and opera.

Family poverty sent him to the tuition-free Jiangnan Naval Academy in 1898, which he left after half a year, and then to the School of Mines and Railways, where he studied English and German and read Western authors. He enrolled at the Sendai Medical College in Japan in 1904 but left medicine for literature.

After holding brief teaching posts, Lu Xun joined the Ministry of Education of the new Republic of China in February 1912 and lived in Beijing from 1912 to 1926. In 1912 he helped design the Twelve Symbols national emblem. In 1918 he published Diary of a Madman, the first novel in vernacular Chinese, under the pen name Lu Xun, taking the surname from his mother. His writing in La Jeunesse after the May Fourth Movement of 1919 brought him prominence.

In Shanghai he lived by writing alone, rejecting regular teaching posts. He turned increasingly to Marxist thought and in 1930 co-founded the League of Left-Wing Writers, though other leftist writers soon accused him of being a feudal remnant and a counterrevolutionary. In 1931 he introduced the woodcuts of Käthe Kollwitz to China. When the Kuomintang passed stricter censorship laws that January, he went into hiding; weeks later it executed twenty-four writers. He died on 19 October 1936 and was buried in a mausoleum in Lu Xun Park in Shanghai, with an inscription in the calligraphy of Mao Zedong.

Lu Xun wrote novels, essays, poetry, translation and political commentary, in both vernacular and literary Chinese. His style mixes sympathetic engagement with ironic detachment, as in The True Story of Ah Q, while My Old Home and A Little Incident are direct. His early novellas often portray weak and frustrated characters who are victims of an oppressive culture, and he criticised what he called the Chinese national character. He judged the Xinhai Revolution of 1911 a failure, and later grew disappointed with the Nationalist government. He championed woodcuts, serial illustrations and cartoons. In China his legacy has been extensively interpreted by the Chinese Communist Party, although in his lifetime he kept a distance from any political organisation.
luanda: Luanda lies on the northern Atlantic coast of Angola and is the country's chief seaport and its administrative, industrial and cultural centre. It has a hot, semi-arid climate, unusually dry for its tropical latitude because the cool Benguela Current keeps moisture from condensing into rain. The old city, the Baixa de Luanda, stands beside the port with narrow streets and colonial buildings, and the Cidade Alta is the newer part.

Paulo Dias de Novais founded the city on 25 January 1576 as São Paulo da Assumpção de Loanda, bringing one hundred families of settlers and four hundred soldiers. The Portuguese built the Fortaleza São Pedro da Barra in 1618 and the Fortaleza de São Miguel in 1634, and the city was their bridgehead in Angola from 1627, apart from a period of Dutch rule, as Fort Aardenburgh, that ended in 1648.

Luanda was the centre of the slave trade to Brazil until the trade was abolished in 1836. Brazilian ships were the most numerous in its port, and local merchants and warriors profited; in 1751 between 5,000 and 10,000 slaves were sold there each year. Angola's ports were opened to foreign shipping in 1844, and by 1850 Luanda was one of the most developed Portuguese cities outside Portugal, exporting palm and peanut oil, wax, copal, ivory, cotton and coffee. It grew from 61,208 inhabitants in 1940 to 475,328 in 1970.

After the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon on 25 April 1974, independence in 1975 and the start of the Angolan Civil War, most white Portuguese residents left as refugees. Migrants fleeing the war swelled the population, and slums called musseques spread far beyond the old limits. The war ended in 2002, and major reconstruction began.

Luanda is the capital and largest city of Angola and holds about a third of its population. Portuguese is the official language, and Kimbundu, Umbundu and Kikongo are also spoken. It is the seat of a Roman Catholic archbishop and the home of most of Angola's universities. Surviving monuments include the Fortress of São Miguel, the best preserved of the colonial forts, Luanda Cathedral and the Palácio de Ferro, and the National Museum of Slavery is in the city.
lubeck: Lübeck lies at the mouth of the Trave, which flows into the Bay of Lübeck at Travemünde. Its historic old town stands on an island and is the southwesternmost city on the Baltic Sea, the closest point of access to the Baltic from Hamburg. The city is in the Holsatian part of Schleswig-Holstein.

A Slavic fortification existed at Old Lübeck, near the confluence of the Schwartau and the Trave, by 819. The settlement, first recorded as Liubice in 1072, became a centre of the Obotrites before it was destroyed in 1138. In 1143 Adolf II, Count of Schauenburg and Holstein, founded a new town on the river island of Bucu. A fire destroyed it in 1157, and Henry the Lion rebuilt it in 1159 and in 1160 moved the bishopric there from Oldenburg. After Henry was outlawed in 1181, Emperor Frederick Barbarossa confirmed its privileges. Lübeck law was later adopted by more than 100 Baltic towns.

In 1226 Emperor Frederick II granted Lübeck imperial immediacy. It lay on the trade routes between the North Sea and the Baltic, and from the mid-13th century other Low German towns asked it to represent their common interests, so that it became the leading city of the Hanseatic League. The League concluded the Peace of Stralsund in 1370, when its power in the Baltic was at its height, and its last diet met in Lübeck in 1669, though it was never formally dissolved.

French troops occupied Lübeck after the Battle of Lübeck on 6 November 1806, and it was part of the First French Empire from January 1811 to December 1813. The Congress of Vienna recognised it as a sovereign free city in 1815. It lost its status as a state on 1 April 1937. A British air raid on 28 March 1942 caused a firestorm that destroyed nearly 1,500 houses and severely damaged the historic centre.

Lübeck has about 220,000 inhabitants. Its old town, designated a World Heritage Site in 1987, is Germany's most extensive. Six church towers exceed 100 metres, and St Mary's Church, built from 1265 to 1351, served as the model for most of the Brick Gothic churches in the Hanseatic sphere. The Holstentor was built from 1464 to 1478.
lublin: Lublin lies in eastern Poland on the Lublin Upland, about 153 kilometres south-east of Warsaw. The Bystrzyca river, a tributary of the Wieprz, divides the city into a western part with loess gorges and a flat eastern part. It is the largest Polish city east of the Vistula and the second-largest city of historical Lesser Poland.

Settlements existed on the site from the sixth to seventh centuries. The stronghold on Old Town Hill was probably one of the main centres of the Lendians, a Lechitic tribe. When it was destroyed in the 10th century the centre shifted north-east and, after the mid-12th century, to Castle Hill.

The Polish–Lithuanian Union of Krewo in 1385 contributed to the city's growth. Lublin lay on the route between Vilnius and Kraków, and in 1392 King Władysław II Jagiełło granted it an important trade privilege. The largest trade fairs of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth were held here, and the Sejm met in Lublin several times in the 16th century. On 26 June 1569 it proclaimed the Union of Lublin, which united Poland and Lithuania. In 1578 the city became the seat of the Crown Tribunal, the highest appeal court of the Commonwealth. A Calvinist congregation was founded, and Polish Brethren made it a centre of Unitarianism.

After the Third Partition of Poland in 1795 Lublin fell to the Austrian Empire, then to the Duchy of Warsaw, and in 1815 to Congress Poland in the Russian partition. A railway link to Warsaw built in 1877 spurred industry. German forces occupied the city in 1939 and it became part of the General Government.

Lublin is the capital of Lublin Voivodeship, created in 1999. Its Old Town, with narrow cobbled streets and a largely medieval layout, is one of Poland's national monuments. The city's institutions include the Maria Curie-Skłodowska University, the John Paul II Catholic University of Lublin and the National Museum of Lublin in the castle.
lucknow: Lucknow stands on the Gomti River, which meanders through the city and divides it into the Trans-Gomti and Cis-Gomti regions. It lies in the middle of the Indus-Gangetic Plain, surrounded by rural towns and villages, among them the orchard town of Malihabad and Kakori.

According to one legend the city is named after Lakshmana, a hero of the Ramayana, who is said to have had a palace or estate there called Lakshmanapuri. The settlement was known as Lakhanpur or Lachhmanpur by the 11th century, and later as Lucknow, the anglicised form of the local Lakhnau.

From the 6th to the 4th century BCE Lucknow was part of Kosala, one of the 16 Mahajanapadas of the late Vedic period. From 1350 onwards it and parts of the Awadh region were ruled in turn by the Delhi Sultanate, the Sharqi Sultanate, the Mughal Empire, the Nawabs of Awadh, the British East India Company and the British Raj. The Nawabs of Lucknow took that name after the reign of the third Nawab, when Lucknow became their capital.

In 1856 the East India Company moved its troops to the border and annexed Awadh, alleging maladministration, and placed it under a chief commissioner. Lucknow was one of the major centres of the Indian Rebellion of 1857. It also took an active part in the independence movement. At the Congress session of 1916 Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru and Muhammad Ali Jinnah met for the first time, and the Lucknow Pact was signed.

Wajid Ali Shah, the last Nawab of Awadh, was a patron of Kathak, a classical dance form that is said to have originated in Lucknow. Under royal patronage the bawarchis and rakabdars, the chefs and royal cooks, developed the Nawabi cuisine of Awadh, with its slow dum cooking. The city's culture comes from the blending of its Hindu and Muslim rulers, and it is known for the ghararas of the Nawabs of Awadh and for chikankari embroidery.

Lucknow is the capital of the state of Uttar Pradesh and the administrative headquarters of its district and division. It had a population of 2.8 million at the census of 2011. It has been the headquarters of the Indian Army's Central Command since 1 May 1963, and it has a bench of the Allahabad High Court. Its monuments of the Nawabi era include the Bara Imambara, known for its Bhul Bhulaiya, the Chota Imambara and the Rumi Darwaza. UNESCO has named it a City of Gastronomy.
lucretius: Almost nothing is known for certain about the life of Lucretius. The only sure point is that he was a friend or client of Gaius Memmius, to whom his poem is addressed. Ancient notes give conflicting hints. A passage in the Life of Virgil attributed to Aelius Donatus says that he died on the day Virgil assumed the toga virilis, but its consular dating is internally inconsistent. Saint Jerome, writing four centuries later, records his birth under the 171st Olympiad and gives his age at death as 43, which would place his birth in 99 or 98 BCE.

Jerome also says that Lucretius was driven mad by a love potion, wrote his books in intervals of insanity, which Cicero later emended, and killed himself. Scholars now accept that this report is inaccurate, and often explain it as confusion or anti-Epicurean bias. Lucretius was probably a member of the aristocratic gens Lucretia and was expensively educated in Latin, Greek, literature and philosophy.

His only known work is De rerum natura, usually translated as On the Nature of Things. Written in some 7,400 dactylic hexameters and divided into six untitled books, it sets out Epicurean physics. It covers atomism, the nature of the mind and soul, sensation and thought, the development of the world, and a range of celestial and terrestrial phenomena. Lucretius is the first writer known to have introduced Roman readers to Epicurean philosophy. In his account the universe runs on physical principles and chance, not on the intervention of the traditional Roman gods.

The poem also sketches the development of humankind, from a life like that of wild beasts through huts, fire, clothing, language, family and city-states. Lucretius proposes that weapons and tools passed from hands, nails and teeth to stones and branches, then copper and bronze, and finally iron. He is believed to be the first to put forward this succession, which was revived in the nineteenth century and linked to the three-age system formalised by C. J. Thomsen from 1834.

In February 54 BCE Cicero wrote to his brother Quintus that the poems of Lucretius showed many flashes of genius and great mastery. The poem influenced the Augustan poets, above all Virgil in the Georgics and the Aeneid, and Horace. It was almost lost in the Middle Ages and was rediscovered in 1417 in a monastery in Germany by Poggio Bracciolini.

It later played a part in the development of atomism, and Pierre Gassendi drew on it. Figures of the Enlightenment also used it in efforts to construct a new Christian humanism. Its account of nature experimenting over long ages, in which the best-adapted creatures survive, has been compared with later thought on evolution, although Lucretius did not hold that new species arose from earlier ones.
ludwig-van-beethoven: Beethoven was baptised on 17 December 1770 in the Catholic parish of St. Remigius in Bonn. There is no authentic record of his birth date, though there is a consensus, with which Beethoven himself agreed, that it was 16 December. His grandfather, also named Ludwig van Beethoven, came from Mechelen and rose to be Kapellmeister at the court of the Archbishop-Elector of Cologne. His father, Johann, a tenor in the same establishment, was his first music teacher, from his fifth year, in a harsh and intensive regime.

Of seven children born to Johann, only Ludwig and two younger brothers, Karl and Johann, survived infancy. Aware of the successes of Leopold Mozart with his children, Johann tried to promote his son as a child prodigy, claiming on the posters for his first public performance in March 1778 that Ludwig was six, when he was seven. He later had other teachers, including Christian Gottlob Neefe. He found relief from a dysfunctional home with the family of Helene von Breuning.

At 21 he moved to Vienna, which became his base, and studied composition with Joseph Haydn. He gained a reputation as a virtuoso pianist and was soon patronised by Karl Alois, Prince Lichnowsky, which led to the three Piano Trios, Op. 1, in 1795, the earliest works to which he gave an opus number. He composed the Pathétique Sonata in 1798, around the time he began to experience hearing loss.

His career is conventionally divided into three periods, a division proposed as early as 1818. In the first he wrote in the classical style of Haydn and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, and his First Symphony premiered in 1800. In the middle period, 1802 to 1812, he developed a distinctive style. The Third (Eroica) and Fifth Symphonies premiered in 1805 and 1808, and his opera Fidelio in 1805. The late period, 1812 to 1827, includes the Missa solemnis and the Ninth Symphony, both premiered in 1824, and the late string quartets.

After several months of illness that left him bedridden, Beethoven died on 26 March 1827, aged 56. The Ninth was the first major example of a choral symphony, and Brahms's First Symphony quotes its Ode to Joy theme. Alex Ross writes that the professional orchestra arose largely as a vehicle for performing Beethoven's symphonies and that the art of conducting emerged in his wake. His nine symphonies are the origin of the so-called curse of the ninth, a superstition that composers were doomed to die before finishing a tenth.

Bonn has a Beethoven House museum in the place of his birth and has hosted the Beethovenfest since 1845. In Vienna, the Beethoven Museum in Probusgasse is where he wrote the Heiligenstadt Testament, and the Pasqualatihaus was his most enduring residence there.
ludwig-wittgenstein: Ludwig Josef Johann Wittgenstein was born on 26 April 1889 in Vienna. His father, Karl Wittgenstein, meant his sons to become captains of industry and had them educated at home; three of the five brothers later took their own lives. After the disappearance and presumed suicide of Hans in 1902, Karl allowed the two youngest sons to attend school, and in 1903 Ludwig entered the Realschule in Linz. From 1906 he studied mechanical engineering in Berlin. Wanting to study with Gottlob Frege, he followed Frege's advice and arrived unannounced at Bertrand Russell's rooms at Trinity College, Cambridge, on 18 October 1911.

After Karl's death in January 1913 he inherited one of Europe's largest fortunes and gave much of it to poets and artists. At the outbreak of the First World War he volunteered for the Austro-Hungarian Army. In 1916 he was posted to the Russian front, where he directed artillery fire from an observation post and was awarded the Military Merit Medal with Swords on the Ribbon. He finished the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus in August 1918; it appeared in German in 1921 and in English in 1922. In the 1920s he taught in Austrian village schools, where his use of corporal punishment caused controversy.

He returned to Cambridge in 1929, offered the Tractatus as his doctoral thesis, and in 1939 was elected to the chair of philosophy that G. E. Moore had resigned. He became a British subject on 12 April 1939. During the Second World War he worked as a porter at Guy's Hospital in London, and he came back to Cambridge for the last time in October 1944.

The Tractatus is concerned with the logical relationship between propositions and the world. Wittgenstein held that what can be said by propositions must be separated from what can only be shown. It influenced the Vienna Circle, although he was never a member.

His later thought, set out mainly in the Philosophical Investigations, published in 1953 after his death on 29 April 1951, rejected many assumptions of the Tractatus. He asked readers to think of language as a multiplicity of language games and argued that, in a large class of cases, the meaning of a word is its use in the language. His papers amount to an estimated 20,000 pages.
luhansk: Luhansk lies in the Donets Basin, or Donbas, in eastern Ukraine, at the confluence of the Luhan and Olkhova rivers. Its name comes from the Luhan River, and a folk etymology links it to the word for meadow, referring to the river's floodplains. The city's main street is Sovetskaya Street, and its central venue for public events is Theatre Square. Several universities have their home there, including a medical university.

The population was 20,400 in 1897 and reached 505,000 in 1992. The census of 2001 recorded 49.6 per cent of inhabitants as ethnically Ukrainian and 47 per cent as Russian, with 85.3 per cent giving Russian as their native language.

The city traces its origin to a foundry set up under a decree of Catherine II in 1795-1796, building ammunition and cannon for the Black Sea Fleet. The British industrialist Charles Gascoigne is credited with founding it in 1797. The works grew during the Napoleonic and Crimean Wars. In 1882 the factory and the neighbouring settlement of Kamianyi Brid were merged as Luhansk, which received city status. In 1896 the German industrialist Gustav Hartmann founded a locomotive-building company there, operational from 1900.

The city changed hands several times in the civil war and was taken by the Red Army in January 1920. On 5 November 1935 it was renamed Voroshilovgrad after Kliment Voroshilov. The name Luhansk was restored in 1958 and replaced again in 1970, after Voroshilov's death, until 1990. German troops held the city from 14 July 1942 until the Red Army liberated it on 14 February 1943. The population rose from 72,000 to 212,000 between 1926 and 1939.

Luhansk was the administrative centre of Luhansk Oblast in independent Ukraine. In 2014 pro-Russian separatists seized the city and made it the capital of the self-proclaimed Luhansk People's Republic, and the Ukrainian regional administration moved to Sievierodonetsk. Russia claimed to annex the oblast in late 2022. Its industries have included locomotive building and metalworking, and it is twinned with Cardiff, Lublin and Saint-Étienne, among others.
luis-de-camoes: Much of what is told about the poet's life is doubtful, and part of it is probably folklore, for only a few dates are documented. His family had its origins in the Kingdom of Galicia. On his father's side he descended from Vasco Pires de Camões, a Galician troubadour, warrior and fidalgo who moved to Portugal in 1370 and received offices, honours and lands from the king. Vasco's son Antão Vaz de Camões served in the Red Sea and married Dona Guiomar da Gama, a relative of Vasco da Gama.

Camões sailed east aboard the carrack São Bento, in the fleet of Fernão Álvares Cabral, which left the Tagus on 24 March 1553. A storm off the Cape of Good Hope destroyed the other three ships, and he landed at Goa in 1554. He entered the service of the viceroy Afonso de Noronha and fought against the king of Chembé. In 1555 he accompanied Manuel de Vasconcelos against the Moors in the Red Sea, and the squadron wintered at Ormuz.

In December 1567 he embarked for Mozambique on the ship of Pedro Barreto, to wait there for passage to Lisbon. Early biographers say Barreto made false promises. The chronicler Diogo do Couto found him two years later so poor that friends fed him, and Barreto embargoed his departure over a debt of two hundred cruzados, which friends paid. He reached Cascais on 7 April 1570. Contemporaries describe him as blind in his right eye, skilled at physical exercises and quick to fight.

His work falls into lyric, epic and drama. Os Lusíadas takes its title from Lusitania, the Roman name for Portugal, and tells how Vasco da Gama and the Portuguese sailed round the Cape of Good Hope and opened a new route to India. Couto recorded that Camões finished it at Mozambique and lost to theft another book, the Parnasum.

His lyrics, scattered in manuscripts, were collected after his death as the Rimas, published in 1595. They include sonnets after Petrarch, odes, elegies, eclogues from Virgil and the Italians, and redondilhas. He wrote three comedies, El-Rei Seleuco, Filodemo and Anfitriões, though the attribution of El-Rei Seleuco is disputed. Torquato Tasso, Cervantes and Goethe praised him.
lusaka: Lusaka stands on the central plateau of south-central Zambia at about 1,280 metres. It lies on the boundary of the territories of two peoples, the Lenje to the north and the Soli to the south, and the main roads of the country, the Great North Road and the Great East Road, cross here. The first known village dates to about the 11th century, a settlement of round huts near the modern suburb of Olympia. In the 19th century slave traders from the coastal regions enslaved members of the Soli and Lenje communities, who moved often to evade them and left no major permanent settlements.

The modern city dates from 1905, when the British South African Company, which controlled Northern Rhodesia, built a railway to link its Copperbelt mines with Cape Town. Lusaka was a water stop on that line, named after a local Lenje chief called Lusaaka. White Afrikaner farmers settled in the area and made it a regional trading centre.

In March 1929 the Colonial Office recommended moving the capital of Northern Rhodesia from Livingstone, citing communications and health. The governor James Maxwell and David Alexander chose Lusaka for its place on the railway and at the crossroads of the two great roads, and the town planner Stanley Adshead confirmed the site in late 1930. The report confirming Lusaka as the planned capital was approved in July 1931. Building went on through the 1930s but was slowed by a shortage of funds. A report of 1938 noted that of 10,000 Africans living in the city only 1,500 were in formal housing, since Africans were permitted to live there only on temporary work permits.

Lusaka lost some status to Salisbury when it became capital of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland in 1953. After a campaign for majority rule led by Kenneth Kaunda's United National Independence Party, Northern Rhodesia became independent as the Republic of Zambia in 1964, and Lusaka was named its capital. A large building programme followed, including government buildings, the University of Zambia and a new airport, and migration from rural areas created many unplanned settlements.

Lusaka is the capital and largest city of Zambia, with 2,204,059 inhabitants at the 2022 census, and the seat of its government. English is the official language. The city centre lies around Cairo Road, and the University of Zambia, founded in 1965, is the country's oldest and largest institution of higher learning. Its people come from all parts of Zambia, and a hybrid called Town Nyanja is widely spoken.
luxembourgish: Luxembourgish belongs to the West Central German group of the High German languages and is the primary example of a Moselle Franconian language. It is closely related to Transylvanian Saxon, which the Transylvanian Saxons have spoken in central Romania since the High Middle Ages. The National Library of Luxembourg has described the Codex Mariendalensis, a poem of nearly 6,000 lines about the life of the 13th-century Yolanda of Vianden, as the earliest known text in Luxembourgish. It was discovered in 1999 at Ansembourg Castle. The language was considered a German dialect until about the Second World War, and then created its own standard form in vocabulary, grammar and spelling.

Luxembourgish has three genders and three cases, nominative, accusative and dative. The genitive survives only in a few phrases, and its work is normally done by the dative with a possessive, as in dem Mann säi Buch, literally the man his book. Like German and Dutch it is a verb-second language. Women and girls are most often referred to with the neuter pronoun hatt. It has borrowed many French words, and its newest vocabulary comes from English. Several dialects exist, grouped into North, East, South and Center forms, and mobility and mass media are leading gradually towards a standard Luxembourgish.

Luxembourgish is the national language of Luxembourg and one of its three administrative languages, with German and French. About 400,000 people speak it worldwide. It is also spoken in the Arelerland region of Belgium, where French has since nearly replaced it, and in small parts of Lorraine. Proposals for a standard spelling go back to the middle of the 19th century. The first official system, adopted on 5 June 1946, won little approval. The standard that became official on 10 October 1975 grew out of the Luxemburger Wörterbuch, published in five volumes from 1950 to 1977, and was modified in a reform of 30 July 1999.
luzon: Luzon covers 109,964.9 square kilometres, which makes it the fifteenth largest island in the world. The South China Sea lies to its west, the Philippine Sea to its east and the Luzon Strait to its north. The Cordillera Central, which holds the island's highest mountain, Mount Pulag at 2,922 metres, and the Sierra Madre enclose the Cagayan Valley, where the Cagayan River, the longest in the Philippines, flows. The name is thought to come from lusong, a Tagalog word for the large wooden mortar used to hull rice.

Fossils of Homo luzonensis from Callao Cave, from at least 50,000 to 67,000 years ago, represent an extinct archaic human species. Before 1000 CE the Tagalog, Kapampangan and Pangasinan peoples had established coastal polities, notably Maynila, Tondo and Namayan. The Laguna Copperplate Inscription, written in 900 and the oldest known Philippine document, names places around Manila Bay. These kingdoms were thalassocracies based on trade with neighbouring Asian states, and Portuguese sailors recorded the island as Luçonia.

Spanish rule began with an expedition sent by Miguel López de Legazpi, which reached Albay in 1569. After the defeat of the local Rajah Sulayman, the capital of the colony was moved from Cebu to Manila. The Philippine Revolution against Spain began in Cavite and spread across Luzon, and the First Philippine Republic was established at Malolos in Bulacan. It lost the Philippine–American War to the United States, which set up Baguio as a summer retreat.

Luzon holds Manila, the national capital, and Quezon City, the most populous city, and the economy of the island centres on Metro Manila. More than half of the people of the Philippines live in the Luzon island group. Most of its languages belong to the Philippine group of Austronesian; Tagalog, Ilocano, Central Bikol, Kapampangan and Pangasinan are the major regional ones. Roman Catholicism is the main religion.
lviv: Lviv lies on the edge of the Roztochia Upland, about 70 km east of the Polish border and 160 km north of the eastern Carpathians. Its highest point is the Vysokyi Zamok, or High Castle hill, which rises 409 m above sea level and overlooks the historic centre with its green-domed churches. The city has been known by many names, among them Lwów in Polish, Lemberg in German, Lvov in Russian and Leopolis in Latin.

In the 14th century Lviv became the heart of Red Ruthenia and Galicia, overtaking older cities such as Halych, Chełm, Belz and Przemyśl. It was the capital of the Kingdom of Galicia–Volhynia from 1272 to 1340. In the wars over the succession King Casimir III of Poland captured the city in 1340 and burned the old princely castle, and Poland gained control of Lviv and its region in 1349. On 17 June 1356 Casimir moved the city to a new site and granted it Magdeburg rights, under which a council elected by the wealthy citizens decided city matters. In 1358 it became the seat of a Roman Catholic archdiocese.

After the First Partition of Poland in 1772 the Habsburg monarchy annexed the region, and Lemberg became the capital of the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria. Its population grew from about 30,000 in 1772 to 196,000 by 1910, with urban poverty alongside the growth. After the First World War the city became a battleground between the Polish population and the Ukrainian Sich Riflemen, and on the night of 31 October to 1 November 1918 the Western Ukrainian People's Republic was proclaimed with Lviv as capital. In the interwar Second Polish Republic Lwów was, after Warsaw, the second cultural and academic centre, home to the Lwów School of Mathematics.

The Red Army entered Lwów on 22 September 1939, and the city became the capital of the new Lviv Oblast. After the war it remained in the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, and most of the remaining Polish population was expelled to the former German territories, especially Wrocław. Since 1991 Lviv has been part of independent Ukraine.

Lviv is the largest city of western Ukraine and the administrative centre of Lviv Oblast. It has Lviv University and Lviv Polytechnic. Its historic heart has cobblestone streets and Renaissance, Baroque, Neoclassicist and Art Nouveau architecture, and is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
lyndon-b-johnson: Lyndon Baines Johnson was born on 27 August 1908 in a small farmhouse on the Pedernales River near Stonewall, Texas. In 1931 Representative Richard M. Kleberg appointed him his legislative secretary, which was Johnson's formal introduction to politics. In 1937 he won a special election for Texas's 10th congressional district on a New Deal platform and served in the House until 1949.

In 1948 Johnson won the Democratic primary for the Senate in a highly controversial runoff against the former governor Coke Stevenson, and then the general election. He became Democratic whip in 1951 and in January 1953 Senate Minority Leader, the most junior senator ever chosen for the post; he became majority leader in 1954. John F. Kennedy beat him for the 1960 Democratic presidential nomination, then offered him the vice presidential place on the ticket to balance it and attract Southern votes.

Kennedy was assassinated on 22 November 1963, and Johnson took the oath on Air Force One that day. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 followed, as did the Revenue Act of 1964. By early 1964 he used the name Great Society for a programme of anti-poverty measures, health care reform, education, urban renewal and environmental protection. After the violent attack on marchers at Selma on 7 March 1965, known as Bloody Sunday, he sent voting rights legislation to Congress. The Social Security Amendments of 1965 created Medicare and Medicaid.

On Vietnam, when he took office there were 16,700 American military personnel in South Vietnam, and Johnson came to support escalation, determined to prevent the spread of Communism. After reports in August 1964 of attacks on two US destroyers in the Gulf of Tonkin, he obtained the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution on 7 August 1964, giving blanket approval for the use of force.

Johnson began his presidency with near-universal support, but his approval fell as the public grew frustrated with the Vietnam War and with domestic unrest, and a gap appeared between what he said and what was happening in the war, which came to be called the credibility gap. After disappointing results in the New Hampshire primary he withdrew his candidacy in 1968. He retired to his Texas ranch and died on 22 January 1973. Historians' judgements of him rest on his legislative achievements on one side and the failure of his Vietnam policy on the other.
lyon: Lyon lies at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône, to the northwest of the French Alps. The two rivers converge south of the historic city centre and form a peninsula, the Presqu'île, bounded by two large hills to the west and north and a large plain to the east. Place Bellecour stands on the Presqu'île. The northern hill, La Croix-Rousse, is known as the hill that works because it is traditionally home to many small silk workshops. The western hill, Fourvière, is known as the hill that prays, because it holds the Basilica of Notre-Dame de Fourvière, several convents and the Archbishop's residence. East of the Rhône a large flat area holds much of modern Lyon and most of its population.

The name evolved from the Gallic Lugdunon, through Lugdon and Luon, into the present form, Lyon, during the 13th century. The Gallic Lugdun, in Roman times Lugdunum, combines two words. The first may be the name of the Celtic god Lug, or lugon, meaning crow, the messenger of Lug, or another word lug, meaning light. The second is dunos, meaning fortress or hill. The name may thus designate the hill of Fourvière, on which the ancient city stands, and could mean hill of the god Lug, hill of the crows or shining hill. Julius Pokorny instead associates the first part with an Indo-European radical meaning dark, black or swamp.

Below the hill, in the present Saint-Vincent district, was the Gallic village of Condate, probably a hamlet of sailors or fishermen on the banks of the Saône. Condate is a Gallic word meaning confluence. In Roman times the city was called Caput Galliae, the capital of the Gauls. During the Revolution, on 12 October 1793, a decree of the Convention Nationale renamed it Commune-Affranchie, meaning Emancipated Commune, and it resumed its name in 1794 after the end of the Terror.

Lyon is the prefecture of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region and the seat of an archbishopric whose holder bears the title of Primate of the Gauls. The districts of Old Lyon, the Fourvière hill, the Presqu'île and the slopes of the Croix-Rousse are inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Roman ruins near the Fourvière Basilica include the Ancient Theatre and the Odeon, and the Amphitheatre of the Three Gauls also survives.

Auguste and Louis Lumière pioneered cinema in the city in 1895. Each 8 December the Fête des lumières marks thanks to the Virgin Mary, who purportedly saved the city from a deadly plague in the Middle Ages, and residents place candles at their windows.
lyuh-woon-hyung: Lyuh Woon-hyung, known by the art name Mongyang, was born on 25 May 1886 in Yangpyeong, Gyeonggi Province, into the Hamyang Yeo clan. In 1907 he joined the National Debt Repayment Movement, and around then he became a Protestant and an associate of the American missionary Charles Allen Clark. In 1910 he broke with tradition by freeing the slaves of his household. He entered the Pyongyang Presbyterian Theological Seminary in 1911, and in 1914 went to China, where he studied English literature at a university in Nanjing before moving to Shanghai in 1917.

In Shanghai he founded in 1918 what became the Shanghai Korean People's Association and led the New Korean Youth League. In 1919 he took part in drawing up the February 8 Declaration of Independence in Tokyo, a precursor of the declaration that opened the March First Movement, and in efforts to send Korean delegates to the Paris Peace Conference. In April 1919 he was among the founders of the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea.

In 1920 he joined the Korean Communist Party. In 1922 he attended the Congress of the Peoples of the East in Moscow, where he met Vladimir Lenin and Leon Trotsky. The Japanese authorities arrested him in Shanghai in 1929 and he served three years in prison. From 1933 he headed the newspaper Chosŏn Chungang Ilbo, and was forced out in 1936 after Korean newspapers erased the Japanese flag from pictures of the Olympic gold medallist Sohn Kee-chung. In 1944, expecting Japan's defeat, he organised a secret committee that spread across Korea.

Just before the surrender the Japanese official Endo Ryusaku made contact with him and agreed to release prisoners. The preparatory committee he founded on 17 August 1945 set up over 140 branches in north and south within the month. In October, under pressure from the United States Military Government, he stepped down from the People's Republic and formed the People's Party of Korea. When a movement to unite left and right arose in May 1946 he represented the centre-left, and was attacked from both extremes.

On 19 July 1947 he was killed in Seoul by Han Chi-geun, a 19-year-old who had fled from North Korea and belonged to the White Shirts Society, a right-wing terrorist group. His death was widely mourned. He is one of the few modern Korean politicians revered in both South and North Korea, and on 21 February 2008 South Korea awarded him the Order of Merit for National Foundation posthumously.
